articles.title: Arch Manning Is Silencing The Doubters, And Texas Is Reaping The Rewards
articles.summary: Arch Manning has faced familiar doubts before. After another slow start, the Texas quarterback is finding his rhythm again — and reminding everyone why expectations were so high.
articles.body: History has a tendency to repeat itself, and Texas fans are witnessing it firsthand with the play of quarterback Arch Manning. It was just a season ago when Manning was tumbling down projected draft boards following disappointing early-season showings against Ohio State and Florida. The Longhorns fell to 3-2 and head coach Steve Sarkisian was making public statements in defense of his quarterback. The questions surrounding Manning were growing louder. Then, following a Week 8 game against Kentucky, everything changed. Manning's season began to take off as he settled into a rhythm and showcased his confidence and command of the offense. He finished his junior year with wins over in-state rival Texas A&M and Michigan in the Citrus Bowl, restoring confidence in his ability to lead the Longhorns to a future national championship. Fast-forward to this season, and the familiar narrative is unfolding again. Arch Is Silencing The Doubters … Again Following back-to-back losses last month to Oklahoma and, ironically, Florida, concerns about Manning's ability to live up to his name came back to the forefront. After the Longhorns' 27-24 loss to Florida, Sarkisian said "everything is going to be evaluated." When asked about a potential quarterback change, Sarkisian doubled down: "Everything means everything." Then came a report that backup quarterback KJ Lacey would receive more first-team reps during practice the following week. Sitting at 4-2, with their College Football Playoff hopes already in jeopardy, Manning gutted out a tough win over then-No. 10 Ole Miss, breathing life into what was starting to look like a lost season for Texas. Now, the Longhorns have won three straight, and Manning has accounted for nine touchdowns during that stretch. The improvement has been noticeable. Manning is getting through his progressions more quickly, with an average time to throw of 2.76 seconds over the last three games — nearly a half-second faster than earlier in the season. That has been a big development. His footwork also looks cleaner and more efficient. Check out this beauty: Or how about this one: After throwing for more than 200 yards just three times in his first six games this season, Manning has now eclipsed that mark in three consecutive weeks. In a world that often lacks patience, we tend to forget that this was an offense replacing five starters from a year ago, with a recruiting class that included more transfer portal additions than any other during Sarkisian's tenure. This offense was always going to take time to come together, and unfortunately, Manning has borne the brunt of the blame. That isn't to deflect from Manning's inconsistencies. There's no doubt he's forced some throws and appeared lost at times while waiting for receivers to separate downfield. The offensive line has been inconsistent and struggled to protect him. The run game has also dealt with injuries and is averaging one fewer first down per game, which brings up another point: Manning is running less. Maybe that's a conscious effort to become more comfortable playing from the pocket, but he's averaging 20 fewer rushing yards per game than he did a year ago. And remember, this was a Texas offense that featured a special package specifically designed to take advantage of Manning's athleticism during the Quinn Ewers era in 2024. Having played quarterback, I know the spotlight is always on you. When things are going well, everyone wants to talk about you. When things aren't going well, everyone wants to talk about you even more. Manning understands that, and given the name on the back of his jersey, he's prepared to handle it. After slow starts in back-to-back seasons, he's been able to block out the noise and rebound, giving his team a shot at the CFP. This week will be Manning's toughest test for the remainder of the regular season: a night game against No. 14 LSU in Death Valley. The outcome will go a long way toward determining the Longhorns' playoff hopes and shaping the narrative surrounding their quarterback. Based on how Manning has responded, I wouldn't bet against him. One Name To Know … Ty Dieffenbach, UCLA If you're looking for the underdog story of this college football season, we’ve got one. The UCLA Bruins are one of just two remaining undefeated FBS teams, led by a quarterback who began the year third on the depth chart. Ty Dieffenbach is a former three-star recruit out of Agoura Hills, California, who began his career at University of Pittsburgh. During the two years he was there, he didn’t see the field and was even asked to move to tight end, which prompted his desire to transfer. Dieffenbach found a home at Cal Poly, where he earned a starting role. However, injuries, inconsistent play and a poor season saw the Mustangs finish 4-8 and led to Dieffenbach looking for a new home. He had a strong belief he could play for a major college football program, and the arrival of head coach Bob Chesney at UCLA provided the chance. Fresh off his CFP run with James Madison, Chesney was billed as the second coming of Curt Cignetti. Following training camp, Dieffenbach moved up to second string. There were even some murmurs that the coaching staff thought he threw the best ball on the roster. Dieffenbach's first snap at the FBS level would come in the second half of one of UCLA's biggest games of the season. Starting quarterback Nico Iamaleava suffered a leg injury in the second half against Oregon, which prompted Dieffenbach to enter the game. He was only asked to throw six times but led a drive in the fourth quarter that created enough cushion to allow the Bruins to pull off the upset. Let the Cinderella season begin. Since that upset, UCLA has continued to rip off wins with a formula that will look familiar to many in Bloomington: a dominant rushing attack, which ranks No, 1 in the Big Ten, combined with a suffocating defense, allowing just 14 points per game. Dieffenbach has managed the offense well and continued to gain confidence each week. He throws a beautiful ball and excels at layering passes against zone coverage. For a 6-foot-6 signal-caller, Dieffenbach has a compact motion and stride with plenty of arm strength. Not to be confused with a dual-threat QB, but he’s a very capable runner and evades pressure to create out of the pocket. It’s impressive to watch his movement in the pocket and the feel he has navigating the pocket under duress. Take a look at this touchdown pass from Dieffenbach in the Bruins' win over Minnesota: Inexperienced quarterbacks have a tendency to bring their eyes down when they have to move off the spot in the pocket. Dieffenbach moves and resets while still maintaining vision downfield to take a shot, then throws a beautiful ball to UCLA wide receiver Aidan Mizell in stride for the touchdown. I’ve been hesitant to write about Dieffenbach until he was able to get over some of those "firsts." First start. First start on the road. First chance for defensive coordinators to see a few games and game plan against him. Well, here we are. The Bruins currently sit at 9-0 and continue to improve and make believers out of me and many others in the college football world. Now if we could just get some of their fans to show up to their games. What I'm Watching … Utah at Arizona Speaking of firsts – "Big Noon Kickoff" is headed to Tucson this week for the Wildcats' Big 12 battle with the only other remaining undefeated team in the nation, Utah. This is essentially a Big 12 championship elimination game for Arizona, a program that has no room for error. This matchup also features two offenses with quarterbacks that exude different styles of play and took different paths to stardom. This will be a homecoming of sorts for Utah QB Devon Dampier, who will be returning to his home state where he played high school football. He began his career at New Mexico, appearing in nine games as a freshman and making one start. He would eventually take over the following year as the full-time starter, becoming the first QB in program history to rush for over 1,000 yards in a season. Former Utah offensive coordinator Jason Beck – yes, the one that just got fired at Michigan – was courted to Utah and Dampier followed. He didn’t quite eclipse 1,000 yards in his first season with the Utes, but he improved dramatically as a passer, earning Big 12 Offensive Newcomer of the Year honors. Despite Beck moving on to Michigan with former Utah head coach Kyle Whittingham, Dampier stayed put and now has the Utes sitting at 9-0 and ranked No. 3 in the nation. On the other side is Arizona QB Noah Fifita, who leads one of the most prolific passing attacks in college football. Fifita began his career at Arizona and has never left, despite coaching changes and easy access to greener pastures via the transfer portal. Fifita broke out in 2023 and has continued to build with the arrival of Arizona head coach Brent Brennan in 2024. He’s a throwback in every sense of the word. Fifita will occasionally take off and run, but he's more focused on keeping his eyes downfield in the passing game. Given his small stature – he's listed at 5-foot-11, but I'll bet a ham sandwich he doesn’t measure that at the NFL Combine – it’s impressive to watch him find throwing windows from the pocket and maintaining his vision downfield. Fifita will eclipse 12,000 passing yards in his career in this game, which will make him the 50th player to do so in college football history. This should be a fun one in the desert! articles.title: Brunson, Towns and the bench help the Knicks beat the Bucks 117-85 for their fourth straight victory
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Jalen Brunson scored 23 points, Karl-Anthony Towns had 21 points and 16 rebounds, and the New York Knicks beat the Milwaukee Bucks 117-85 on...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Jalen Brunson scored 23 points, Karl-Anthony Towns had 21 points and 16 rebounds, and the New York Knicks beat the Milwaukee Bucks 117-85 on Tuesday night for their fourth straight victory.

OG Anunoby made five 3-pointers and finished with 19 points for the Knicks, who have won six of seven since an 0-3 start. They outscored the Bucks 32-13 in the second quarter to blow open the game and then put it away in the fourth after Milwaukee had gotten back into it.

The Knicks got big efforts from their bench, with no starter playing more than 28 minutes on the front end of back-to-back games. Tyler Kolek scored 12 points and provided a spark in the second quarter as the backup to Brunson, Andre Drummond grabbed 14 rebounds in 15 minutes, and Deuce McBride had eight points and New York outscored Milwaukee by 39 while he was on the floor.

Jaime Jaquez Jr. scored 16 points and Ryan Rollins had 14 for the Bucks, who lost their seventh straight and fell to 1-10. They played without leading scorer Tyler Herro, who missed his first game of the season because of a bruised right knee.

The Knicks led by three early in the second quarter before Anunoby and Kolek combined for the next 10 points to make it 36-23. Ousmane Dieng made a 3-pointer before Kolek scored again to ignite another 10-0 run, and Brunson and Anunoby ended the half with consecutive 3-pointers to make it 58-34.

Milwaukee pulled to 85-72 after three quarters and got the first basket of the fourth, but Towns led the way as New York quickly pushed the lead beyond 20, with consecutive 3-pointers by Anunoby making it 106-78.

Josh Hart missed his third straight game, this time because of an illness. He sat out the previous two because of right ankle soreness, but coach Mike Brown said he believed the starting forward was healed enough that he could have played if not for feeling sick.

Bucks: Host the Los Angeles Lakers on Wednesday.

articles.title: Jeremy Fears Jr. Leads No. 5 Michigan State Past No. 2 Duke In Champions Classic
articles.summary: Jeremy Fears Jr. had 18 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds as No. 5 Michigan State shut down No. 2 Duke for a rugged 79-73 win.
articles.body: Jeremy Fears Jr. had 18 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds as No. 5 Michigan State shut down No. 2 Duke for a rugged 79-73 win Tuesday night. Playing coach Tom Izzo’s usual swarming, physical defense, Michigan State held Duke to 33.3% (20 for 60) shooting from the field and forced 13 turnovers. Jordan Scott had six of the Spartans’ eight blocked shots and two of the team’s seven steals. Cam Ward added 14 points as Michigan State (3-0) earned its first win against Duke since a 75-69 victory on Dec. 1, 2020. The Spartans also improved to 7-9 in the Champions Classic, an annual doubleheader that also includes Kansas and Kentucky in various combinations and different cities early in the season. John Blackwell scored 17 points for Duke (2-1), and Patrick Ngongba II finished with 11. The shooting trouble for the Blue Devils extended to the free-throw line, where they went 26 for 37. Duke opened the regular season with a pair of runaway victories against Army and Coastal Carolina, averaging 98.5 points while shooting a combined 55% from the field. But the Blue Devils looked uncomfortable for most of the night at United Center, home of the NBA’s Chicago Bulls. Jesse McCulloch made two free throws and Fears converted a three-point play to help Michigan State open a 50-36 lead with 13:37 remaining. Duke closed to 73-68 on Caleb Foster’s two foul shots with 2:03 to go. But then Scott responded with a driving layup for Michigan State, and Fears made two free throws with 39 seconds left. Fears drove inside to set up Ethan Taylor’s three-point play late in the first half, lifting Michigan State to a 34-25 lead at the break. Fears had eight assists at halftime, and the Blue Devils shot 25.9% (7 for 27) from the field in the early going. Up Next Duke hosts SIU Edwardsville on Friday night. articles.title: Despite hurt wrist, Antetokounmpo scores 30 and Heat outlast Jazz 115-109
articles.summary: SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, Davion Mitchell added 19 points, and the Miami Heat outlasted the depleted Utah Jazz 115-109 on...
articles.body:
SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, Davion Mitchell added 19 points, and the Miami Heat outlasted the depleted Utah Jazz 115-109 on Tuesday night.

The Heat also got 14 from Pelle Larsson but needed late blocks from Klay Thompson and Bam Adebayo to secure their third win in their last four games.

Antetokounmpo iced his sprained right wrist in a heavy wrap when he was on the bench but it didn't seem to bother him on the court. He shot 12 for 21 and grabbed 11 rebounds.

He now has 21,836 points and passed Gary Payton to become the 39th leading scorer in NBA history.

Despite the Jazz's ninth straight loss, Utah's two teenagers gave the Jazz hope for the future. Rookie Darryn Peterson nearly set his career high (26) for the second game in a row with 25 points and Ace Bailey scored 23.

Utah's Isaiah Collier, a notoriously poor shooter who had not made a 3-pointer this season, made four consecutive shots from behind the arc in the fourth quarter to cut Miami's lead to 101-93.

Then Svi Mykhailiuk made back-to-back baskets to cut the lead to 112-107 in the final minute but it was too late for the Jazz, who were missing four starters to injury — Lauri Markkanen (wrist), Keyonte George (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee), and Jusuf Nurkic (foot).

Antetokounmpo's shooting sparked the Heat to a 15-2 run in the third quarter to give the Heat the cushion they needed and send them home with a 3-2 record on their five-game road trip.

Larsson hit a 3-pointer with 6:58 left in the second quarter to cap a 13-1 run and make it 49-32 for Miami.

The Jazz, who have been hurt by turnovers all season, had 18 to just eight for the Heat.

Heat: Host Cleveland on Friday night to commence a five-game homestand.

Jazz: Host Orlando on Wednesday to complete the back-to-back set.

articles.title: Kings’ Darius Acuff Jr. doesn’t hold back on 1-10 record after loss to Magic
articles.summary: The Sacramento Kings are spiraling early in the season, and rookie point guard Darius Acuff Jr. isn’t trying to sugarcoat the frustration anymore. Sacramento...
articles.body:
The Sacramento Kings are spiraling early in the season, and rookie point guard Darius Acuff Jr. isn't trying to sugarcoat the frustration anymore. Sacramento hit another low point on Tuesday night, falling 107-100 to the Orlando Magic at Golden 1 Center.

The defeat dropped the Kings to a dismal 1-10 record, tying the worst 11-game start in franchise history. Despite the team's ongoing slide, Acuff put on another spectacular individual show. The 18-year-old guard led Sacramento's attack with 29 points, six assists, and four rebounds while playing 40 minutes.

But personal box-score numbers meant very little to the rookie after watching another winnable game slip away in front of the home crowd. Following the loss, beat reporter Frankie Cartoscelli posted on X that Acuff was visibly frustrated while addressing the media. The rookie guard held nothing back when assessing Sacramento's struggles.

"1-10 just don't sound right," Acuff said. "There's nobody to blame but ourselves… We're trying; we're talking as a team. When the clock hits zero and we're losing, that's the most frustrating part."Acuff has shouldered a massive load early, becoming the first NBA rookie since 1983 to attempt at least 20 shots in each of his first 10 career games. He got offensive support from veteran guard Zach LaVine, but Sacramento couldn't string together enough late stops.

Orlando executed key possessions down the stretch, keeping the Kings winless at home with an 0-6 mark. Sacramento's locker room communication has yet to pay dividends on the court. While Acuff continues to show superstar potential, high-scoring nights won't soften the blow for a rookie driven by winning. Until the Kings fix their late-game execution, the frustration in Sacramento will only build.

articles.title: Manchester United Reportedly Nearing Deal To Hire USA Coach Mauricio Pochettino
articles.summary: Mauricio Pochettino is leaving the United States men’s national team for Manchester United.
articles.body: United States men's national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino appears to be Manchester bound. Manchester United are finalizing a deal to hire Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach, if the club decides to sack club legend Michael Carrick following his 1W-5D-4L start to the Premier League season as manager, according to a report from The Athletic on Wednesday. The move comes less than three months after Pochettino signed a four-year contract extension with U.S. Soccer in August, following the USA’s run to the round of 16 at the 2026 World Cup on home soil. To get him out of that deal, United is expected to trigger Pochettino's buyout clause, which is reportedly worth around $10 million. United and U.S. Soccer have yet to make official contact, according to The Athletic's reporting. Pochettino inherits a club in crisis. United sit in the Premier League’s relegation zone after a dismal start to the season under Carrick. United has not been relegated since the 1973-74 season. Carrick, a former United midfielder, was named permanent manager this past offseason after impressing as interim boss following Ruben Amorim’s sacking in January. His permanent tenure lasted less than six months. Pochettino’s first match in charge could be one of the toughest on the calendar. United return from the international break against Liverpool on Nov. 22. The 54-year-old Argentine is no stranger to the Premier League. He led Tottenham Hotspur to the 2019 Champions League final and later managed Chelsea for the 2023-24 season. He also won a Ligue 1 title with Paris Saint-Germain. Pochettino took over the national team in September 2024. His departure leaves U.S. Soccer searching for a new coach ahead of the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, with matches against Haiti on Nov. 14 and 17 in the United States. articles.title: Rio: “No-Brainer Going to Liverpool”
articles.summary: Liverpool’s pathway convinced Rio to switch from blue to red.
articles.body:
Liverpool FC attacker Rio Ngumoha is the subject of a profile in The Telegraph , and there are some pretty interesting quotes in the piece.

The article leads with Harry Kane's Ballon D'or win, and if he thinks he can win it one day. He answered yes, duh.

The rest of it explores Ngumoha's journey from Manor Park, Newham, a borough of London to Chelsea's academy. It's worth a read.

The latter half of the piece gets into Ngumoha's reasons for leaving Chelsea and joining the Reds:

"I feel like I needed a new challenge. I feel like if I stayed at Chelsea… I'm not saying that I wouldn't have got to the first team as quick, because I believe in my ability, but I feel like Liverpool just gave me a new pathway. "The plan that they set for me was straightforward really. For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool, and they just said if I prove myself, because they know how much ability I had, then they know that I would definitely be a first-team player and definitely a star for them in the making. I think going to Liverpool so far has been the right choice."

I think going to Liverpool so far has been the right choice."

Again, he speaks of the sacrifice his mother has had to go through to facilitate his move to Liverpool:

"My mum has done a lot for me. The hardest thing for her has been moving up to Liverpool. She left her job in a school to move up three or four months after me. But I think she's enjoying it as well. It's definitely been tough as she has friends in London. She goes back whenever she can. But she does everything for me and my brother. She's just amazing. I can't thank her enough."

Rio also spoke about his experience with the England national team setup so far, and with Thomas Tuchel specifically:

"When I first came [with England], I was a bit shy, so I was keeping myself to myself," said Ngumoha. "But then they got me in the group. The shyness goes from the first time you touch the ball and step on the pitch. Then you realise it's just football and you can play the way you play. After the first session, it goes." "I think it's very nice. He knows I'm quite talented, which is good. Every time I come on, he lets me be expressive, be free. He also coaches me as well. Off the ball, on the ball, little ideas. I just have the belief from him and all the coaches here. It's top. Hopefully I can just keep going and keep leaving a good impression on him."

articles.title: Cheboygan's Gahn making basketball voice heard in youth community
articles.summary: Cheboygan basketball star Landon Gahn hosted his first youth camp to teach discipline and skills to local kids at the Elite Sports Training gym.
articles.body:
CHEBOYGAN — Just outside the Elite Sports Training gymnasium, you could hear the basketballs bouncing.

Once you got inside, there was one basketball enthusiast making his voice heard .

But instead of absorbing what coaches and camp directors were saying to him, he was the one teaching.

PHOTOS: Cheboygan senior Landon Gahn hosts first youth basketball camp

For the first time, Gahn hosted a youth basketball camp during two different sessions on Sunday, Nov. 8.

"It's awesome. I love helping kids out," Gahn said. "I love basketball and it's just kind of a way to get more kids involved, and for me to be more involved with them because of all the training and knowledge that I've taken in over the years. If I'm not relaying that to the younger generation, then I'm not doing my part as a basketball player and just as a member of the community, really. It means the world."

Whether it was working with 1-3 grade basketball players in the morning session or his time with 4-6 graders in the afternoon, Gahn got his basketball points across to nearly 30 kids who attended the camp.

From dribbling to shooting to defending, Gahn's camp featured many facets of the game.

One area was emphasized a little bit more compared to others, Gahn explained.

"Discipline is the biggest thing, probably," Gahn said. "I like to tell them that all the drills that we do are things that you can go year long, and if you're not doing them year-round, then you're not going to get any better."

When he was younger, Gahn participated in basketball camps that were directed by his father, Nick Hancock, a former Cheboygan hoops standout and owner of Elite Sports Training.

"I really appreciate him teaching me," Gahn said of his dad. "All the drills that I run, I learned from him previously. The fact that we have the opportunity to use this gym is special. We're super lucky to be able to run anything like this."

From start to finish, Gahn's basketball passion was there for every camper to see.

"Just being around coaching, I think coaching might be in my future, and I like the leadership part of that, and I realize that communication and being vocal is being the biggest part," Gahn said.

With his senior season about to begin, Gahn's unquestionably in basketball mode. But even when he's not playing on the court for the Chiefs, he's doing his best to make a difference in the sports community.

"Not just basketball, I just love to be around kids in general, whether it's seeing them at school or here," Gahn said. "I feel like making a little kid's day is the best thing you can do as a person. Just lift them up, so to be able to share my expertise in basketball here while also making them feel good about themselves, that's the best part of it."

Down the road, Gahn would like to run another camp.

And he's hoping to spread the word not just to those in town.

"For anyone that's reading this, the more kids, the better," Gahn said. "This isn't just a Cheboygan thing. If you're in the area and you want to make your kid to get better, we'll help you out."

articles.title: Purdue football's Tra'Mar Harris turns tragedy into breakout success story
articles.summary: Tra'Mar Harris' late sister felt Purdue football was the right fit. After two seasons of not seeing the field, Harris is thriving as a junior receiver in her...
articles.body:
WEST LAFAYETTE − Most run from adversity.

Tra'Mar Harris has been living in it for three years.

After two years with Purdue football, where his only time seeing the field was 13 plays on Nov. 8, 2025 against Ohio State in a game that was for all intents and purposes already decided, Harris considered entering the transfer portal.

After some self reflection, and a full court press by a persuasive Boilermaker coaching staff, Harris realized Purdue was where he was most comfortable.

Somewhere, Deasia Wynn is smiling and shouting her trademark phrase, "that's what's up."

Wynn is a primary reason Harris chose Purdue in the first place. She celebrated her 26th birthday accompanying her little brother on a recruiting visit to West Lafayette. By the end of the night, Wynn told Harris Purdue was the right place for him.

The star receiver at Winton Woods High School in Cincinnati committed to the Boilermakers a week later, choosing them over more than 20 other Division I scholarship offers .

By the time Harris enrolled at Purdue in January 2024 at age 17, his sister had been gone for more than two months, the victim of a cold-blooded murder while in her sleep.

"They were very close. She came to all his games, supported him, took him to practice. He went to her house every other weekend to stay the night," said Tra'Mar's mother, Trina Scott-Harris. "She was like the little momma bear."

Check out our Purdue football vs Illinois photo gallery: Best images

Tra'Mar Harris hurting, healing through football

The Harris household's world revolved around sports. Parents Markus and Trina were athletes. The oldest child, Chuck Wynn, played college football at Eastern Kentucky and Urbana University, and coincidentally enough made his first career tackle against Purdue in Ross-Ade Stadium. Deasia was a basketball standout, a pure shooter with a quick step and unmatched strength that offset her limitations in speed and leaping ability. She played collegiately for Miami University-Hamilton and Ohio State-Mansfield. Her No. 15 is retired at Winton Woods High School. The youngest, Jayden Harris, is a junior at Winton Woods, where he's a multi-sport athlete.

The one athletic feat that will never be matched, though, came from Tra'Mar Harris on Oct. 20, 2023.

It was the day after Deasia Wynn was senselessly shot . At 3 o'clock that afternoon news spread that Wynn was killed at the hands of her childhood best friend. Coaches told Harris he didn't have to play, but the then-senior at Winton Woods needed an escape and football was about to provide it for Harris and his family.

"He decided to play to help us get through it," Markus Harris said. "The first half he probably had 30 yards, and then had 170 yards and two touchdowns in the second half. To have that strength after something like that, I don't know if any of us could've done it, but he was the inspiration for our family in that moment."

From the stands, family members cried. From the sideline, young Jayden celebrated every catch. From the playing field, Harris showed why college football coaches matriculated to Cincinnati in hopes of luring him.

"All I know is I could have used that opportunity to shut down, too. Shut down as a player. Shut down in a lot of different ways, but I did the opposite," Harris said. "I brought my family up. I picked them up, played the Friday night game and had my best game."

In the months that followed, Purdue was a steady presence in the Harris house. Then head football coach Ryan Walters would make drives from West Lafayette to Cincinnati. They'd talk about things that had nothing to do with football. Another week, another Purdue coach at the house.

"It was always someone there from Purdue," Markus Harris said.

Former Purdue quarterback turned wide receiver Bilal Marshall at the time was the receivers coach at West Virginia. Though Harris already was committed to Purdue, Marshall sat in the living room with the family trying to lure Harris away from his alma mater.

Marshall will tell you he almost had him. He didn't know it at the time, but he soon would.

Talent obvious, but breakthrough required time, healing and leap of faith

Tra'Mar Harris enrolled at Purdue early, arriving at 17 years old in January 2024. He was naturally athletic, had good size and long arms. Plenty fast enough to stand out in that first spring.

Still grieving the loss of his sister and navigating the challenges of adapting to college life, Harris never found the field for a football team that went 1-11. After the season, Ryan Walters was fired as head coach and the football staff received an overhaul under new head coach Barry Odom .

Among the hires was an offensive analyst with ties to Purdue, whose duties included working with wide receivers. His name was Bilal Marshall.

Marshall, obviously, already knew of the talents of one player he'd be working with, one he remembered from seeing in high school that had "uber talent."

"Tra'Mar was just a freak of nature on the field. Every football field he stepped on, he was the best football player on the field," Marshall said. "He was still raw and playing with just pure athleticism. He needed to develop as a wide receiver and learn how to run routes. But there was things Tra'Mar could do that a lot of people couldn't."

Little did Marshall know then that after a 2-10 season, he'd have to re-recruit Harris. In 13 snaps against Ohio State, Harris caught two passes for 2 yards, his first collegiate stats but hardly something that through two seasons matched his talent.

On top of that, Purdue wasn't winning, which meant more staff changes. Marshall was elevated to receivers coach . He was in the room when Purdue's staff pleaded with Harris not to make a rash decision based solely on two seasons of riding the bench.

"There were thoughts (of entering the transfer portal) with Tra'Mar," Purdue offensive coordinator Josh Henson said. "We had talks with he and his family and they decided to stick it out. We told Tra'Mar if you'll stick it out, if you'll do that, you'll go develop and get better. We believe in his talent. It's just the production was inconsistent."

On Saturday, Oct. 31, Purdue was playing at Penn State's Beaver Stadium.

It was the first time Tra'Mar Harris was in the starting lineup. It marked the eighth straight game Harris was a piece in Purdue's offense. The 2026 season started, just as it had the prior two seasons, with a victory against a lower-tier opponent.

Something was different on Sept. 4, though. Harris was on the field, playing meaningful snaps in a college football game for the first time. With Purdue leading 23-6 in the third quarter, quarterback Ryan Browne dropped back after taking a snap from the 7-yard line. Browne fired a pass to the goal line near the right pylon. Harris caught it for his first career touchdown, losing all control as his emotions poured out during a celebratory dance.

"I was like, hold up, yes, that was Tra'Mar," Trina Scott-Harris recalled.

It sure was, dancing like a fool in the end zone.

"It meant a lot for me personally," Harris admitted. "I have a sister that I play the game for. I just use her as motivation. So obviously, scoring that first touchdown, she was the first person I thought about, the first thing I thought about. That's why it meant so much to me."

Harris' second touchdown would come in Purdue's second victory , one that broke the Boilermakers' string of 19 consecutive Big Ten losses.

Purdue led Illinois 6-0 late in the second quarter. Browne lofted a ball towards the left sideline, midway into the end zone. Harris slid, readjusted his body and hauled in a 21-yard TD. He had 3 receptions for 52 yards in a 24-17 victory that spoiled Illinois' homecoming.

"Since my freshman year, me and him always talk like he's going to be good," said cornerback Hudauri Hines, like Harris a member of Purdue's 2024 signing class. "We're seeing it now. It's no surprise to me. I knew all along."

"Tra'Mar academically is having the best semester he's ever had," Purdue head coach Barry Odom said. "He has shown practice habits that have resulted in him playing well on game day situations. He's also playing extremely well when he doesn't have the ball in his hands. It's great for him and us that's seeing some reward for that.

"It is a product of if you continue to pour in the right way results will happen. We're just seeing the start of what Tra'Mar is going to be. He's an impact guy."

That sales pitch from the Purdue coaching staff after last season was coming to fruition. While talks that day centered around football, they also involved a consistency of arriving early and performing in the classroom.

In a recent call with his son, Markus Harris said he heard Tra'Mar utter words for the first time.

"He was talking about going to grad school the other day," Markus Harris said. "It felt like he scored 10 touchdowns when he was talking about that. We always held our kids to a standard in the classroom, but to see him hold himself to that and look ahead and say I have something pretty awesome here, and it wasn't centered around football. We love the game of football and hopefully one day he can walk across the stage and get drafted, that would be awesome.

"But we definitely want to see him walk across that stage with multiple degrees in his hand. To see that playing out right in front of your face is pretty cool."

In the summer of 2023, Deasia Wynn knew something nobody else did at the time.

Purdue was the right place for her little brother. It took three years for Tra'Mar Harris to realize she was right all along.

Somewhere, Wynn is laughing and belting out her famous phrase.

articles.title: Missouri football needs to be more committed to running the football
articles.summary: When Mizzou's run game struggles, the Tigers tend to lose. Fixing that issue might be as simple as recommitting to running it for four quarters.
articles.body:
If there's one thing Kirby Smart knows about Eli Drinkwitz's teams …

"Let's be honest, there are teams that don't commit to the run. (Eli Drinkwitz) is committed to being stubborn with it," the Georgia coach said Monday. "… Their commitment to the run game and downhill runs helps them be who they are."

Smart's right. When the Tigers get hardheaded with that wide zone, they've historically been a tough out.

But, heading into a matchup with the No. 1 Dawgs on Saturday, Nov. 14, in Athens, Mizzou might need to renew those vows.

"I think the first thing we have to do is be more committed to the run," Drinkwitz said Tuesday. "I think 19 carries for a tailback, especially in that kind of game (against Texas) — we can do more in that run game."

In a 34-20 loss to Texas on Saturday — and in both of Missouri's other two defeats this season — the ever-reliable run game has struggled. How well the Tigers are able to run the football, especially in the second half, has been one of the clear indicators of success this season.

Jamal Roberts has handled RB1 duties well. He's currently leading the SEC and is No. 5 in the Power leagues with 1,071 rushing yards this year, or 119 yards per game.

But, on three Saturdays this year, the ground game has let the Tigers down.

Take, for instance, just 3.5 yards per carry for 84 total rushing yards in Saturday's loss to the Longhorns. Mizzou has been held below 4 yards per carry in three games this season, and you can probably guess the three games: Texas, Ole Miss and Mississippi State. All losses.

Missouri getting back to what it does best isn't necessarily as simple as just doing it more, but there's some positive correlation here.

The games against the Longhorns and Rebels, perhaps not coincidentally, also happen to be the games Mizzou has taken its fewest rushing attempts this year.

"Talking about a bit before, the biggest thing with run blocking is when you come out of a game and you get 3, 4 yards a carry, that's just the beginning of giving body blows in a fight," MU center Dominick Giudice said, "and as time goes on in the game, you'd be able to wear teams down. Obviously, we weren't able to do that this past game.

"That's a challenge going forward — being able to get those body blows going on teams early, and then being able to break ones later in the game."

Roberts has been good at that, when given the chance.

Drinkwitz said, even with Ahmad Hardy back in practice and available to play, that Roberts will continue to be the Tigers' workhorse this year. Roberts has taken the most carries of any running back in college football this season, and — at his best — does some of his most productive work in the second half.

The plan is still to get Hardy back into action.

The All-American, who has taken three carries in two games and been on the field for nine snaps since returning to play Oct. 31 from an offseason gunshot wound to his leg, had opportunities against Texas that could have resulted in runs, Drinkwitz said, but the Tigers opted for throws on the RPO plays.

"There will be guys who can rotate in with (Roberts)," Drinkwitz said, "but if we're only going to have 19 carries for backs, maybe 22 carries total for the backs, as of right now, I would say he's going to get 19 or 20 of them."

Drinkwitz seemed to indicate that the Tigers want more than between 19-22 carries.

Missouri has averaged 5.6 yards or more per carry three times this year, in wins over Florida, Texas A&M and Arkansas. In those games, MU ran the ball at least 35 times.

Now, you call what's working, you avoid what's not.

But … Mizzou was averaging 2.3, 4.6 and 4.2 yards per carry at halftime in those three games. Mizzou's rushing success rate was not above 43% for the full contest, which, according to Hudl IQ's advanced analytics , is lower than the season-average of every single SEC team.

The Tigers stuck with it and benefitted after halftime for three SEC wins. It doesn't need to work on every single play if it creates some explosives later in games.

"I think there is the cumulative effect of making sure that we land body blows throughout the game," Drinkwitz said. "We've got to continue to do that."

It's understandable why the Tigers have strayed from the run at times.

In the Texas and Ole Miss games, Mizzou was chasing late in the game. That naturally means throwing the football more often and a generally lopsided run/pass ratio.

But the Tigers are giving up some of their best chunk plays in the process. Mizzou has hit a 20-yard run in every single one of its wins over an FBS team this year. It has not hit an explosive of that distance in any of its losses — the games it has run the football the least.

The Tigers (6-3, 3-3 SEC) have likened what they want to do running the football to boxing matches: body blows, wear and tear, late KO.

Georgia's next, and the Bulldogs (8-1, 6-1) are as strong as they come up front in the country this year.

So, Mizzou had better rediscover its love for committing to the run.

"Just being able to stay ahead is obviously something we want to do," Giudice said, "and being able to maybe hit those big runs early on in the game, being able to make sure, obviously, we're gonna get the 3, 4 yards, which is what we want, but being able to hit those earlier on in the game to be able to stick with that, I think would be, obviously, the best way to do it."

articles.title: Roma could revive Leweling interest in January as Stuttgart lower asking price
articles.summary: Last summer, Jamie Leweling was linked with a move away from VfB Stuttgart, but he ultimately stayed put after the German side rejected a €35 million offer p...
articles.body:
Last summer, Jamie Leweling was linked with a move away from VfB Stuttgart, but he ultimately stayed put after the German side rejected a €35 million offer plus bonuses from AS Roma shortly before the transfer window closed.

Stuttgart invested €55 million in new signings, and the club's supervisory board has now decided that player sales will be necessary to balance the books.

According to Bild, Leweling is among the players who could be sold – and potentially as early as January.

The German tabloid reports that Stuttgart are now willing to let the winger leave for a fee of around €30 million, having lowered their asking price.

Reports in Italy suggest that Roma are still looking to strengthen their options out wide, so it would not be surprising if the Serie A club's decision-makers once again considered a move for the 25-year-old.

articles.title: La historia de Michael Schumacher y su reloj Casio de 1.500 pts que sacaba de quicio a sus ingenieros
articles.standfirst: El alemán lo llevaba pegado a los volantes de sus Benetton de Fórmula 1 pese a que ni siquiera tenía función de cronómetro, ya que que para él era muy importante
articles.summary: El alemán lo llevaba pegado a los volantes de sus Benetton de Fórmula 1 pese a que ni siquiera tenía función de cronómetro, ya que que para él era muy importante
articles.body: Broad Arrow es una casa de subastas que no pasa demasiado tiempo sin sacar a la venta lo que los aficionados al motor llaman 'memorabilia', que explicado de forma resumida son objetos que guardan algún tipo de relación con el mundo del automovilismo. Pero, entre los muchos lotes que va sacar a subasta el próximo 22 de noviembre en Francia, nos ha llamado la atención uno que en apariencia no puede ser más sencillo: se trata de un volante que por sus formas parece sacado de un kart. Pero no es de un kart, sino de un Fórmula 1, y en su centro luce un humilde reloj Casio que puso ahí quien se encargaba de gobernar el coche, que no fue otro que Michael Schumacher. El volante pertenece a un Benetton B195, un coche animado por un motor Renault RS7 V10 de 3,0 litros que entregaba 760 CV con el que el alemán consiguió su segundo título de pilotos, además de que otorgó al equipo el campeonato de constructores. Y el reloj que lleva en el centro, simplemente pegado, se trata de un Casio F-30, un modelo de la gama inferior del fabricante japonés que cuando salió al mercado en 1991 costaba algo menos de 18 marcos en Alemania (unas 1.500 pesetas en España, que equivalen a 9 euros). Viéndolo en el volante de un Fórmula 1, uno daría por hecho que cuenta con cronómetro. Tal vez incluso con temporizador de cuenta atrás. Pero ni una cosa ni otra; al parecer, al Kaiser no le resultaba fácil manejar los diminutos botones de un reloj pequeño con los guantes de piloto, así que el alemán se limitaba a consultarlo sin otra cosa en la pantalla que la hora, los minutos y los segundos. Pero, ¿para qué lo necesitaba? Debemos tener en cuenta que en 1995 los volantes diferían mucho de los que empezamos ya a ver en el nuevo siglo, ya con pantallas que entre otras cosas empleaban la telemetría del coche para mostrar los tiempos por vuelta. Y también que la comunicación del piloto con boxes no ofrecía entonces la calidad con la que hoy día los pilotos se comunican con su equipo en el muro. Por ello, Schumacher aprendió a apañarse por su cuenta, quizá también porque estaba acostumbrado a hacerlo en su época anterior a la Fórmula 1. Lo que hacía era ver y memorizar el minuto y el segundo exacto en el que cruzaba la meta, y a raíz de ello controlaba mentalmente los parciales de cara a conseguir la mejor vuelta en la calificación, así como si estaba mejorando o empeorando su ritmo ya en carrera, lo que le permitía anticiparse a las órdenes que le pudieran dar. Esta confianza en su memoria, y en un reloj que parecía pensado para un niño de 12 años, generó durante años cierta incomodidad entre su equipo técnico, que veía cómo el alemán dedicaba parte de su atención a comprobar los tiempos en un reloj barato y a hacer cálculos en lugar de centrarse al 100% en la conducción y dejar que su equipo le diera los tiempos exactos. Uno de esos volantes es el que ahora saca a subasta Broad Arrow. Es plano por debajo, está forrado de ante por completo (salvo en su sección central) y cuenta con cuatro botones recubiertos de goma. Eso sí, aquel coche incorporaba cambio por levas y las dos paletas que permitían subir y bajar de marcha no están junto al volante. Los coleccionistas valoran mucho cuando un objeto que ha pertenecido a un Fórmula 1 (o un Fórmula 1 entero) ha participado en carrera. Y más si a ello se suman aspectos tan importantes como que haya subido al podio o conseguido una victoria. En este caso, un Certificado de Autenticidad expedido por Benetton Formula 1 Racing Team acredita que el volante fue tan solo empleado en test, sin aludir a que lo usó Michael Schumacher porque la presencia del reloj ya acredita que así fue. Quizá por esto último, se espera que el precio de venta se sitúe entre los 10.000 y los 12.000 euros.

articles.title: Pakistan women’s captain Fatima Sana calls for gender equality in cricket
articles.summary: Fatima Sana ‘dreams of a time’ when the men’s and women’s cricket teams are treated as equals.
articles.body:
Pakistan cricket captain Fatima Sana has called for parity between the country’s men’s and women’s teams, urging fans to show greater support for female players by filling stadiums for their tournaments.

The 25-year-old says she “dreams of a time” when the Pakistan women’s cricket team are treated as equal to the men’s team. “I hope it comes,” Sana said on Tuesday.

Sana, who has led the Pakistan team since 2024, is one of the country’s finest cricketers and has swiftly risen to the top echelons of women’s cricket.

The all-rounder is playing franchise cricket for the Australian Perth Scorchers in the Women’s Big Bash League (WBBL) in Australia, one of the world’s top women’s cricket competitions.

Following her team’s six-wicket win over Melbourne Stars on Sunday, Sana was asked about the state of women’s cricket in Pakistan.

“If you look at world cricket, the sport is growing,” Sana told digital cricket news platform CricBlog TV.

“I would like to see the same growth in Pakistan, be it in the men’s or women’s game.”

The right-arm medium-fast bowler is the second Pakistani player to feature in the WBBL after former captain Nida Dar, who played for Sydney Thunder in 2019.

Sana, who holds the world record for the fastest international 50 in women’s T20 cricket, led Pakistan to a bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

“The way the crowds turn up for men’s matches, I hope the same happens for the women’s matches,” she added.

Sana hopes for more Pakistani representation in WBBL

Since making her WBBL debut on October 31, Sana has picked up five wickets in as many matches, with a bowling economy of 7.62 runs per over – figures that keep her joint-10th in the most-wickets chart.

Her WBBL campaign marks just the second time the 25-year-old has featured in an overseas league, having also played for Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred in England.

“It is an honour to come here and have the opportunity to play [in Australia]. It’s great to play alongside my teammates; they’re very supportive and helpful,” Sana said.

“Personally, I wish for more and more girls from Pakistan to come and play in Australia so that cricket can grow back home in Pakistan, too,” she added.

At Perth Scorchers, Sana shares the dressing room with some of the world’s best players, including ex-New Zealand captain Sophie Devine and Australia batter Beth Mooney.

Pakistan will host the next edition of the women’s T20 World Cup in 2028. It will also be the first to feature 12 teams, up from 10 in the previous six editions.

It will be the first ICC women’s event held in Pakistan, which has hosted two ICC Men’s ODI World Cups and the ICC Men’s Champions Trophy in 2025.

Sana believes the tournament could help boost women’s participation in the sport in the cricket-mad South Asian nation.

“It’s a great step by the ICC that the [2028] World Cup is taking place in Pakistan, which will encourage more women players to come forward,” Sana said.

“When more girls watch the World Cup at home, their parents will also offer them more opportunities to play the sport.”

articles.title: El drama del dopaje infantil: "Pueden ser en torno a 10 millones de niños, es un gran problema"
articles.standfirst: Una investigación de la televisión pública alemana ARD revela la magnitud del dopaje de millones de niños en un documental por capítulos que se emitirá a partir del viernes
articles.summary: Una investigación de la televisión pública alemana ARD revela la magnitud del dopaje de millones de niños en un documental por capítulos que se emitirá a partir del viernes
articles.body: Una nueva investigación realizada por la televisión pública alemana ARD revela la dramática magnitud del dopaje infantil en todo el mundo, una denuncia que aumenta la presión sobre los organismos deportivos para que tomen medidas contundentes al respecto. Después de seis años de trabajo, en los que se analizaron 44 estudios basados en encuestas confidenciales realizadas en 15 países, el equipo encabezado por el periodista Hajo Seppelt demuestra que entre los 195 y 260 millones de niños y jóvenes (entre 8 y 17 años) que participan en deportes de competición, según Naciones Unidas, en torno a 10 millones estarían afectados por el dopaje. Esto se extrapola del hallazgo de que un 5%-6% reconocía haber utilizado sustancias dopantes."Existe un problema enorme y no se está haciendo nada al respecto", ha asegurado a la cadena germana Paulo David, exsecretario del Comité de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos del Niño. Según revela el reportaje, existen numerosos indicios de que este dopaje infantil a nivel mundial es mucho más generalizado, ya que muchos menores no admiten el consumo de sustancias en las encuestas o incluso son dopados a veces sin su conocimiento, con sustancias que ellos creen de forma errónea que son inofensivas y están permitidas. Además, se produce también una infradetección de positivos en los controles a deportistas menores. Así, la magnitud del dopaje infantil a nivel mundial contrasta con el número de jóvenes que dan positivo: apenas 100 al año en todo el mundo, lo que significaría que solo el 0,001% de los casos son detectados. Esta serie documental de ARD, que empezará a emitirse este viernes 13 de noviembre, proporciona pruebas directas de que entrenadores, directivos, padres y médicos dopan a menores con el objetivo de ganar medallas y dinero. Además, muestra cómo la desesperación de los niños ante la constante presión por triunfar los lleva a recurrir a sustancias dopantes, que en muchos casos tienen consecuencias a largo plazo.

articles.title: Man City whistleblower Rui Pinto could help UK uncover more sporting crime
articles.summary: Rui Pinto is ‘in talks’ with UK authorities to help uncover more crime in exchange for police protection, reports say.
articles.body:
Football whistleblower Rui Pinto , whose leaks triggered an investigation into Manchester City’s financial misconduct , has held discussions with authorities in the United Kingdom over a new role in helping uncover financial and sporting crime in the country, reports in British media say.

Pinto’s lawyers have been contacted by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) after he stated he would be willing to assist UK authorities with investigations in exchange for police protection, British newspaper The Guardian reported on Wednesday.

Al Jazeera sought confirmation of Pinto’s reported contact with the authorities, but the SFO did not confirm whether the whistleblower was in talks.

“In line with long-established practice to avoid prejudice to law enforcement activity, we can neither confirm nor deny any investigation into this matter,” the SFO said in an emailed statement to Al Jazeera.

Pinto appeared to confirm the reports of his discussions with the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) by reposting an article on his social media account.

The 38-year-old is the founder of the website Football Leaks, which obtained private documents that showed City broke league rules from 2009 to 2018, leading to a probe by the Premier League’s independent commission.

City were found guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against them over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Pinto’s lawyer, William Bourdon, who has represented other high-profile whistleblowers including Julian Assange and Edward Snowden, was quoted by the Guardian as saying: “I can confirm that the process is under way.”

Pinto said last month that he feared for his life after being told his witness protection programme would end on October 10 and launched a crowdfunding initiative to help him establish an anonymous new life.

“The Commission responsible for Portugal’s witness protection programme informed me of its decision to terminate my participation in the programme and withdraw my police protection, thereby knowingly placing me in a life-threatening situation,” he wrote in a social media post.

“Given these circumstances, I have no alternative but to relocate, within the next few days, to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period of time, due to the multiple death threats I have received and the serious risk of an assassination attempt against me.

“For this reason, I have just set up a GoFundMe campaign and I am asking for everyone’s support to help me survive this serious situation created by the Portuguese State, which, as I have already stated, has knowingly decided to place my life at risk.”

However, the Portuguese Ministry of Justice said it would extend his protection pending a new hearing, after Pinto’s lawyers challenged the decision.

Reports last month said Pinto had reached out to UK authorities to offer cooperation in ongoing investigations in exchange for security measures being placed around him.

Pinto said at the start of his trial in April 2020 that he was “proud” to be a whistleblower on European football clubs’ big-money dealings.

The former history student and self-taught computer expert faced 90 charges – from unauthorised access to data and violation of correspondence to attempted extortion – in the case heard at Lisbon’s Central Criminal Court.

“I don’t consider myself a hacker. I am a whistleblower,” he said at the time. “The revelations are serious and I’m proud; there’s no shame. I haven’t done anything for money,” added Pinto, who acknowledges releasing 70 million documents on football’s backroom workings.

He was given a four-year suspended sentence in September 2023 for illegally obtaining documents, committing other cybercrimes and attempted extortion. He was later acquitted on 241 separate counts in a second trial in April 2026 after the court ruled the charges were ­­“invalid”.

Pinto has been a protected witness since August 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest. His first trial in Portugal began a month later.

articles.title: Luke Littler: World number one expected 'pub player' opponents on Netflix show
articles.summary: Luke Littler says he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-changing money".
articles.body:
Luke Littler has admitted he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-changing money".

Broadcast live globally on the streaming platform last month, the cash was won by top women's player Fallon Sherrock.

The format of 'Beat Luke Littler' saw 24 players selected to take on the world number one in a single leg of 501, hoping to win a prize of £501,000.

The 24-strong field did include low-level opponents, such as an Australian jockey, a bin man and a Nando's manager, but anyone who was not a member of the PDC Tour was also allowed to compete.

That meant Sherrock - who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019 - and leading junior players Mitchell Lawrie and Zach Griffiths were also eligible.

"Before I saw the line-up, I thought it was just pub players," said Littler, who is preparing for the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.

"Whereas obviously when the line-up came out, I probably knew just over half of them.

"Mitchell, Zach Griffiths - I played with him on the Development Tour - obviously Fallon, Katie Sheldon and a lot more.

"I mean Fallon, she's never had a Tour card, so she went for the qualifiers and she made it through. But then she wasn't guaranteed to play - she went in on a vote."

Sherrock, who has been awarded an MBE for her services to darts, made it through an audition process and then had to rely on the public to select her to take on Littler at Manchester Central.

Littler beat 14 contestants but then lost to Sherrock, who won nearest the bull to throw first and then checked out in 15 darts.

"It was a very good night overall," Littler added. "I think from my side it was very good. From Netflix's side, it was very good.

"I think the whole thing was probably a learning curve. For me, constantly playing back-to-back, especially in the heat, I was going off and on stage. I'm up for another one and I'm sure Netflix will be as well.

"There aren't many people who could say they've got their own show, and I've had my own show on Netflix, which is just still bonkers to me."
