articles.title: 50 Ideas to Fix the Sports World, from Realistic to Galaxy-Brained
articles.summary: Every sports fan knows not to expect perfection. In fact, it's just the opposite: The games we love come with cracks, blemishes and irregularities.
articles.body:
Every sports fan knows not to expect perfection. In fact, it's just the opposite: The games we love come with cracks, blemishes and irregularities.

And that's OK. We're here for it anyway.

But that doesn't mean we can't strive toward the Platonic ideal—or at least wail into the ether about the cosmic injustices we're forced to witness with agonizing regularity.

In that spirit, the B/R staff both pitched their own flaw-fixing ideas and scoured the digital landscape for creative thoughts from fans and other media members.

What resulted was a wide field of thoughts, from realistic to creative to galaxy-brained. We're not saying every one of these entries will be implemented by the sport in question, but it sure would be fun if they were.

All Leagues: Give Fans Veto Rights in Superstar Trades

The Problem: We're all about direct democracy here at Bleacher Report. Power to the people, not the puppet masters.

Bottom line: We think fans should have a bigger say in major decisions.

We think it's unacceptable that a few high-ranking people can trade away beloved icons for future draft compensation. Nobody likes this.

The Creative Fix: Give season-ticket holders and other registered fans the right to veto the trade of a franchise icon within 48 hours of an agreed-upon deal.

They'd have to reach a 70 percent supermajority. The block could only be used once every five years on players who achieved multiple All-Star or Pro Bowl nods or at least one MVP in the past five seasons. That player would then be ineligible to be traded for three years after the veto.

Some pro teams—like the Green Bay Packers and European soccer clubs like Barcelona and Real Madrid—have dipped their toes into a system of fan involvement in ownership and governance. This would simply be an extension of that.

We imagine a world where qualifying players must be deemed expendable by fans, for a collectively agreed-upon price. GMs and owners can try to sell fans on trade ideas, and players can still request trades.

But Luka's staying put if Luka wants to be there. Don't even @ us with the Micah trade proposal. And no more crying kids in their obsolete Jaylen Brown Celtics jerseys.

All Leagues: Bring Relegation to US Sports

The Problem: Too many American sports fans are left with little or nothing to root for in any given year by midseason or sooner because of tanking or general ineptitude. European soccer fans don't have to deal with this, as even those stuck with loyalties to bottom dwellers experience the unparalleled tension and thrill of a relegation battle.

The Creative Fix: Expand all major American pro sports leagues and institute a first and second division where teams get promoted and relegated each year. In so many ways, this is better for fans and athletes.

Let's start with the ways this benefits fans. More teams in more places means more opportunities for fans to see games. Next, tanking is immediately a thing of the past. No one has to put up with intentional losing. Lastly, there are rarely meaningless games, as nearly every team would be fighting to get into a playoff spot or stay out of the relegation zone for most of the season.

All those things also benefit athletes. More teams mean more jobs for players. No more tanking and fewer meaningless games mean those jobs are more interesting and exciting.

Now, let's get to who this might not be good for: owners. Relegation means owners aren't guaranteed the revenue that comes with a non-negotiable spot in the top division. It's hard to imagine American sports owners allowing this to happen because of that short-term loss, even though there's a good case to be made that it would have a long-term financial benefit to leagues.

But we're not here to get bogged down in what would or wouldn't make owners more money. Relegation would be fun for fans and athletes. That's more than good enough for us to believe it should happen.

The Problem: What's worse, tanking or hearing everyone complain about tanking for the 40th straight year?

It's time for everyone to shut up a little bit.

The Creative Fix: Galaxy-brained redditor kelownafornia6969 (seriously) has a frothy solution: dynamic beer pricing to fix NBA tanking.

The idea went viral. It hasn't left our brains.

In kelownafornia6969's words: "The rule: set beers at $10 for all teams at the start of the season. Teams can increase prices by $0.35 per win and MUST decrease prices by $0.20 per loss. "

So last year, Wizards fans would've been paying $2.95 for a beer (or, let's say, ice cream as another option), while OKC fans would've been paying close to $30 for one.

Honestly, hard to say which game I'd rather attend (and obviously, we'd endorse non-alcoholic solutions for the NA/underage crowd).

Now, would a front office be persuaded by a beer subsidy? Probably not.

But remember, this is really about shutting up the yelling-at-cloud folks with a dose or two of beer/ice cream/whatever. Who says no?

All Leagues: Allow the No. 1 Seed to Pick Its Opponent

The Problem: Thanks to injuries, an otherwise-loaded team sometimes barely manages to sneak into the playoffs. It then becomes the vaunted lower seed that none of the top contenders want to face. But is that fair to the No. 1 seed, who might have a tougher first-round matchup than lower-seeded teams?

The Creative Fix: Allow the No. 1 seed to pick its opponent in each playoff round. If the No. 1 seed has a bye, the highest-seeded team in that round picks its opponent.

There are two clear benefits here. First, the No. 1 seed gets more fairly rewarded for being the best team in the regular season. It shouldn't have to rely on the luck of the draw to avoid a would-be No. 4 seed that wound up being a No. 8 seed. By getting to pick its opponent, the No. 1 seed can choose the path that maximizes its chances of making it to the next round.

Or so it thinks, anyway. The other benefit here is the hilarity/slander factor. Whichever opponent the No. 1 seed picks gets instant bulletin-board material. If that opponent proceeds to pull off the upset, it'll be a top-five day on social media.

NBA teams have pitched this idea before, according to Zach Lowe , but it went nowhere. MLB recently proposed it as well, as part of its ongoing negotiations over its next collective bargaining agreement.

Once one major league does it, don't be surprised if others quickly fall in line. It's going to be electric.

The Problem: Cowards, basically. With field-goal kickers now able to boot 60-plus-yard field goals with relative ease, teams should rarely (if ever) punt once they get past the 50-yard line. However, old-school Boomers like Andy Reid still haven't caught on yet .

The Realistic Fix: Look to the UFL for a solution. In 2026, it adopted a rule that prohibits teams from punting once they cross the 50-yard line, even if "a subsequent penalty or loss of yardage moves the ball behind the 50." (This rule does not apply in the final two minutes of either half, though.)

This would—or should, anyway—completely change play-calling around midfield. Once a team crosses the 50 and can't punt, getting stuck in a 3rd- or 4th-and-long would have far more downside. Teams might opt to run the ball more or favor shorter completions instead of attempting to air it out, at least until they got into field-goal range.

If a team turns the ball over on downs around midfield, its opponent would only need to travel about 20 yards to get into reasonable field-goal range. Since the NFL appears to be in a constant hunt for ways to juice scoring, this would be one of the easiest changes to make, especially since it would reduce the likelihood of a team getting pinned inside its own 10-yard line after a punt.

The Surrender Index would be far less active on Sundays, but never underestimate the cowardly nature of NFL coaches. They'd find new ways to chicken out instead of improving their team's chances of winning games.

NFL: Swap the Onside Kick for 4th-and-15

The Problem: The NFL's "dynamic kickoff" revitalized the kick-return game, but it ruined onside kicks. Teams now have to declare their onside attempt, removing the potential element of surprise. As a result, the success rate of those plays has plummeted in recent years .

The Realistic Fix: Scrap onside kicks entirely and replace them with a 4th-and-15 for the offense. That idea might sound gimmicky, but it's been floating around the NFL for years . (Hall of Famer Drew Brees is already on board .)

According to CBS Sports' Jonathan Jones , the NFL "would prefer" that teams have a 12 percent chance of success on onside kicks. Jones added that "NFL data suggests a 4th-and-17 play has a success rate around 12 percent, so that could be the sweet spot for such a play."

The United Football League also implemented a version of the NFL's dynamic kickoff ahead of the 2025 season. Concurrently, it eliminated onside kicks and gave teams the option to attempt a 4th-and-12 play from their own 28-yard line instead. Teams went 3-of-7 on such plays through the first eight weeks of the regular season, although two of those three conversions resulted from defensive penalties.

Leads have become far less safe in the NBA due to the volume of three-point shooting these days, which makes games more exciting. What once looked like an insurmountable deficit can now be overcome within a quarter or a half. Changing the onside kick rule to give offenses a better chance of coming back late in games would have a similar impact on NFL games. When those 4th-and-?? attempts go awry, the opponent would take over possession in field-goal range.

The Problem: NFL teams converted only 41 percent of their two-point attempts in 2024, according to Greg Auman of Fox Sports, which was a 15-year low. They also went for two-point attempts only 9.8 percent of the time after touchdowns. Per Auman, 72 percent of those came in the fourth quarter. A majority were passing plays, too.

The Realistic Fix: Right now, two-point attempts begin on the 2-yard line. Moving them up a yard to the 1-yard line could increase teams' incentive to go for them more often, and it should also increase the success rate on those plays.

NFL fans who've grown sick of the Tush Push might recoil at this proposal, but in general, two-point attempts are far more exciting plays than a kicker attempting a 33-yard extra-point kick. Besides, the Philadelphia Eagles have become far less adept at the Tush Push in recent years, following Jason Kelce's retirement and their offensive line injuries.

NFL teams converted their 4th-and-1 attempts at a 71 percent clip in 2024, according to Auman , so the math would heavily support going for it every time. But if teams did decide to eschew extra points entirely, defenses would spend more time figuring out ways to thwart those two-point attempts as well.

If nothing else, this would be a way for skill-position players to get extra fantasy football points. And who doesn't love more fantasy points?

NFL: Cap Pass Interference at 15 Yards, No Flags on Underthrows

The Problem: Pass interference occurs when "any act by a player more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage significantly hinders an eligible player's opportunity to catch the ball," according to the NFL's rulebook . If an offensive player commits pass interference, it's a 10-yard penalty. If a defensive player commits pass interference, the ball moves to the spot of the foul, which incentivizes quarterbacks to chuck deep balls and pray for a flag.

The Realistic Fix: Pass interference should be capped at 15 yards. The NFL doesn't have to look far to find a reasonable compromise to this problem.

In college football, if PI occurs within 15 yards of the line of scrimmage, the ball is placed at the spot of the foul, making it an automatic first down. If it happens more than 15 yards past the line of scrimmage, the ball gets moved 15 yards downfield and it's an automatic first down.

In 2018, the New York Jets proposed adopting a version of that rule , although pass interference would have remained a spot foul if the contact was "intentional and egregious." (The UFL adopted that version in 2024 .) However, it did not gain enough support from the competition committee.

The NFL has already juiced scoring by moving touchbacks to the 35-yard line and making changes to the balls used for field goals. As much as we all love fantasy football points, defenses are increasingly at a disadvantage compared to offenses due to recent NFL rule changes. Switching to the college football PI rule would help restore some balance.

Also, if a quarterback throws a duck and a defender gets tangled up with a receiver trying to decelerate, that should be a no-call. Hit the gym and drink some protein shakes, bud.

The Problem: If a team fumbles the ball at its opponent's 1-yard line and it goes out of bounds, it maintains possession at the spot of the fumble. If a team fumbles the ball at the goal line and it goes out of the end zone, its opponent takes possession at its own 20-yard line. Make it make sense .

The Realistic Fix: A team should not lose possession for fumbling through the back of the end zone. That's the bottom line. Let's start there before going into the nuance of this proposed fix.

With that said, there should be some sort of punishment for an offensive player fumbling out of the end zone. Otherwise, they'd have more incentive to extend the ball out once they get close to the goal line, which would put beleaguered defenses at even more of a disadvantage.

What if the NFL flipped the touchback rule on its head? Offenses could still maintain possession of the ball after a fumble out of the end zone, but they'd have to move back to their opponent's 20-yard line with a new set of downs. Worst-case scenario, they'd still be in field-goal range (barring a turnover), but they don't get to just Tush Push their way into a touchdown after fumbling at the goal line.

This rule has already come into play during the playoffs . It's only a matter of time before it swings a critical game. In 2024, a league source told CBS Sports' Jonathan Jones that the competition committee had not discussed changing it, but the NFL could eventually regret that.

NFL: Losing Team Picks the 4th-Quarter Wind

The Problem: Going into the fourth quarter, a team's direction is already settled. If the losing side is headed straight into the jaws of gale-force winds, it could end the chances of a rousing comeback before it gets started. Who doesn't want more late-game tension?

The Creative Fix: Allow the losing side to choose its direction at the end of the third quarter, making the weather a bigger part of the strategy and potentially increasing drama.

If there's a tie after the third, keep the normal field-direction rotation. Ditto for a dome. But things would get interesting as the winter months near in places like Chicago, Cleveland, New England and Buffalo, among others. The sun and glare are also factors, so even warm-weather games could be affected.

Does it punish the leading team for playing well? Slightly. But the opponent still has to earn the win, as it also increases the chance for better theater.

The Problem: Remember Cowboys star Dez Bryant's infamous overturned catch in the 2014 playoffs against the Packers? The NFL rewrote its catch rule in 2018 to prevent that sort of reversal from happening in the future.

Yet replay keeps flipping big catches. In the 2022 playoffs against the Bills, Bengals star Ja'Marr Chase lost a would-be leaping score at the back of the end zone to the video.

Just last season, the Vikings' T.J. Hockenson had a diving TD overturned by the tape after it was controversially ruled that he didn't maintain ball control. Similarly, the Panthers' Tet McMillan lost a diving fourth-quarter catch in a tie game last December. The league privately told the Panthers it got the call wrong.

Now, a multiple-choice question. All of those plays:

A) were jaw-dropping displays of athleticism

B) created the kind of euphoria fans crave

C) certainly looked like catches to the naked eye

D) were otherwise spectacular plays disallowed because of a technicality only slow-motion replay could reveal

If you guessed E, you see where we're going.

The Creative Fix: If there's any question about a play originally ruled a catch, a replay can only overturn it if it's an obvious mistake viewed at full speed. The ball has to have clearly hit the ground, for example. No frame-by-frame dissections.

Of course, we understand the need for a clear definition of a "catch." We'd simply propose that the naked eye get a bigger say than replay.

There's enough spirit-killing in football with the zillion penalties that can be called. Leave the brilliance alone.

NFL: Replace the Coin Toss with a QB Throw-Off

The Problem: Flipping a coin is your grandparents' way of settling possession and field direction. It's boring and leaves too much to chance. Why not get wild?

The bigger issue is that opposing NFL quarterbacks are never on the field at the same time. That feels like a gaping entertainment gap when it comes to the game's biggest stars.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: Have each quarterback stand behind the same goal line and throw the ball as far as they can, one at a time. Whichever throw lands farthest earns the same privileges as the current coin-toss winner.

QBs would have just warmed up anyway, so the injury risk would be minimal. If that's too much of a concern, let teams designate any thrower they want from the 53-man roster. The amount of hidden arm talent could be dazzling. Or meme-worthy. It would be a must-watch pregame event in the ever-growing litany of NFL sideshows either way.

The Problem: Football has too many obscure rules. None are more inane than procedural penalties like illegal shift and illegal formation. Few things in an NFL game are less fun than a great play getting wiped out by a penalty that even many hardcore fans couldn't really explain.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: As long as an offense doesn't commit a false start, let them do whatever they want before the snap.

Be honest. Do you actually know what constitutes an illegal shift or illegal formation? In our experience, only two types of people answer yes to that question: liars and Hochulis.

Few fans care about or understand these particular rules, so it's hard to see how they add to the game.

If they want to line up with just a center, a QB and nine wide receivers who run in circles 10 yards behind the line of scrimmage, let them! Common sense dictates they probably shouldn't do this, but there's no reason to make a rule preventing it.

Scrapping every pre-snap penalty except false start would allow creative coaches to come up with even more ways to evolve offenses and create cool gadget plays. It'll also allow bad coaches to find new ways to screw up spectacularly, which is still exciting for fans! It also gets the refs out of one more phase of the game, which can only be a good thing.

This change would be addition by subtraction at its finest.

The Problem: Kickers add almost nothing but dumb luck to fantasy football. Fantasy champions can be decided on the foot of Tyler Loop. All a K slot does is add wasted time every week when you use them as waiver fodder and then have to remember to roster a kicker on Sunday.

The Realistic Fix: The tyranny of the K slot must be eliminated. Fix fantasy football by killing K as a default in private and public leagues.

Fantasy kickers are nothing but a nightmare when you lose because your opponent's kicker got busy. It's nothing to be proud of when your team gets that K edge. Kick out the K.

Fantasy Football: Score Defenses on Big Plays Only

The Problem: Standard fantasy scoring penalizes defenses for yards and/or points allowed, which can cause a unit that racks up turnovers to still score close to nothing in a shootout.

Often, a defense's day is ruined by things it can't control, thanks to the offense's turnovers or generally poor field positioning.

The Realistic Fix: Get rid of negative defensive plays from standard scoring and award points for big moments like interceptions, sacks, defensive TDs, etc. Nothing comes off the board.

Sure, any commissioner can set up a league however they want, but people often go with how the major fantasy outlets have things set up. Making this the standard setting does a better job of isolating a defense's day from how its offense performs.

Fantasy Football: Targeted WR Gets 3 Points on Pass Interference

The Problem: When a running back catches a dump-off pass in PPR, it's at least one point. When a wide receiver runs a perfect route 20 yards deep and gets knocked down just before he was going to catch the pass: Zero points.

It makes no sense. The real team advances the ball 20 yards on the pass-interference call, but your fantasy team gets nary a point.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: Not anymore with this sensational solution. Now the fantasy victim of PI gets three points. One for the expected catch and two for a token yardage value, without the fantasy game having to speculate on the actual yardage.

What about a PI that doesn't get called? Or a wide-open receiver whose QB can't throw right? Sorry. Can't help you there.

CFB: Put the CFP Quarterfinals on Campus

The Problem: The first round of the College Football Playoff is held on campus, but the quarterfinals and beyond are held at neutral sites. That means the top four seeds never get a game on campus, while the No. 5 through No. 8 seeds do. On a completely unrelated note, three of the top four seeds lost in the quarterfinals in 2025.

Beginning in 2027, the field will expand to 24 teams . The first two rounds will be on campus, but nothing beyond that.

The Realistic Fix: The CFP should also put the quarterfinals on campus. That would result in a more drastic reimagining of bowl branding—for instance, the Rose Bowl would no longer be in Pasadena every year—but that's a worthy sacrifice to help ensure college football crowns its best team champion each season.

If we're being honest, the days of college football fans caring about bowl branding are a thing of the past. While winning the Rose Bowl, Sugar Bowl and Orange Bowl might have been a point of pride in the past, the only thing that matters now is advancing in the CFP. Beyond that, novelty bowls such as the Pop-Tarts Bowl are the biggest attention-grabbers.

If the CFP eschewed the bowl system entirely—or the bowl sponsors were fine with hosting those bowls on campus instead of neutral locations—the top four seeds would get to reward their fans with a home game. That alone wouldn't necessarily guarantee a victory, but it would ensure that the lower seed didn't have a geographic advantage when it came to fans traveling for the game.

CFB: Require 1 Throwback Uniform for Every Team

The Problem: In a sport that prides itself on tradition, the uniform arms race is too often about blackout themes and metallic looks . Examples abound of teams wearing futuristic fits that eschew the past.

The Realistic Fix: The NCAA should lean into the NIL era and require schools to go retro at least once a year. The unis would act as a nice attention-getter and help schools fund their player pipelines.

It's not just a money grab, though. It's a great way to keep the connection to the past that's so important to the sport. Illinois, for instance, paid homage to Red Grange's 1924 look (pictured above) in 2024, connecting current fans to a great of yore.

If we're talking about teams without much uniform history (or changes), do what other sports do: Conjure some fauxbacks. In other words, make retro-looking jerseys , even if they never existed.

Why? Because throwbacks are fun, and CFB needs to get up to speed. Most pro leagues have their old-school vibes on lock, with the NFL, NHL, NBA and MLB regularly going retro.

Schools get to increase revenue while fans get more Saturday outfit options. Everyone wins.

CFB: Require a Marquee Opener for the Champs

The Problem: While early marquee matchups have become frequent, cupcake openers still happen too often. Look no further than the defending national champ, Indiana, and its 3-0 North Texas-Howard-Western Kentucky stretch in which the Hoosiers dominated 145-16.

The Creative Fix: Mandate that the defending national champion face a strong Week 1 opponent.

The goal would be to make it feel less like a punishment and more like a prize for the challenger. A prove-your-mettle-type power move for those circling the next trophy.

Conference champs can opt in to the pool from which the defending champs get to pick. From that pool, the five highest-ranked teams from the previous season's final AP poll make the shortlist of options to host the game.

Dub the challenger "The Kingslayer," televise the selection and revel while fans and analysts spend the lead-up debating who should get the shot.

The Problem: Flopping has gotten out of control in the NBA. The league tried to address it, making it punishable as a technical foul since 2023-24. But it's been a half-hearted measure, with the rule explicitly stating that players can't be ejected for multiple flopping violations.

The Realistic Fix: The league is off to a good start by seemingly making an effort to enforce its existing rule this season. Now, it should treat flopping like other technical fouls, meaning if you do it twice in the same game, you get the rest of the night off. It's the absolute least that could be done to convince fans there's a real effort to curb this behavior.

The risk-reward proposition, as it currently stands, still feels too much in favor of the flopper. The reward is a turnover and a personal foul against one of your opponents if you successfully dupe the ref. The risk is just giving away one measly free throw, no matter how many times you try it. If you think shame is any sort of deterrent, you probably haven't watched the game in a while.

Something more needs to be done. This would be an exceedingly moderate and reasonable step toward making flopping less part of the game than it is now.

Our other ideas to punish this behavior included allowing floppers to be legally fouled for some period of time and forcing them to change into 1980s-style short shorts for the remainder of the game. So we can and will escalate if "two flops and you're tossed" doesn't get the job done.

NBA: Add a 1-on-1 Tournament at All-Star Weekend

The Problem: The NBA's All-Star Weekend has lost most of its sizzle. The Three-Point Contest is fine, the Skills Challenge is whatever, and the Slam Dunk Contest is mostly populated by random young players or G Leaguers. The league needs something to revitalize All-Star Saturday.

The Realistic Fix: Institute a one-on-one event, pitting star against star.

The NBA has to look no further than Unrivaled, the three-on-three women's basketball league populated by WNBA stars. It introduced a three-day one-on-one tournament in 2025 and ran it back this past year because it was such a hit with fans. In fact, the semifinals and finals of its 2025 tournament drew more viewers (377,000) than Unrivaled had for its opening game (312,000), per Ryan Glasspiegel of Front Office Sports.

Given the amount of player movement throughout the NBA these days—along with the hurt feelings that often come with it—this is an absolute no-brainer for the NBA to replicate. Can you imagine Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum competing in a one-on-one contest? Kevin Durant vs. Anthony Edwards? Joel Embiid vs. Nikola Jokić? The possibilities are endless.

The NBA might not be able to convince every All-Star to compete in a one-on-one tournament, but offering a significant cash prize—or perhaps some free helicopter rides? —could incentivize participation. Whichever company sponsors it should also offer to match each player's winnings with a donation to a charity of their choice.

If the NBA spread out the tournament over two days, it could hold the first two rounds on Friday or Saturday and then do the semifinals and finals the following day. Of course, that would cut into players' ability to attend "brand activations," which is what All-Star Weekend has effectively become, but this would be a way to turn attention away from the league's business partners and back to where it belongs: the fans.

The Problem: Anyone who played a game or two of organized basketball growing up instinctively knows what a travel is. Heck, even people who exclusively played pickup ball seem to have a better idea of the rule, at least by its traditional interpretation, than the NBA currently does.

If you're handling the ball, you get two steps after you stop dribbling. That's it. That's all. But in 2009, the league added the ability to "gather" the ball before taking those two steps. The players have gone miles with that figurative inch since.

NBA players basically moonwalk before shooting step-back threes now. Finishers in transition routinely take four or five steps without dribbling before dunking because, ostensibly, the first few steps are during that nebulous "gather."

This isn't just a petty annoyance (though it is that too). With the way the rule is called, it's simply too easy for offensive players to get an advantage. A defender has done his job when his assignment doesn't have a good look after those two steps. Allowing the ball-handler to just keep walking isn't fair.

The Realistic Fix: Roll it back to the pre-2009 rule. The foot on the floor when a player stops dribbling counts as one step. He gets one more before making a basketball move.

The NBA even had to clean up the language around the rule in 2019 to try to better define the gather. Yet players still boggle the mind with the way they push the traveling limits.

Sure, today's top stars have the extra step built into their games, but defenders adjusted when the hand-check went away, and so will the best scorers.

The Problem: Until 2006, high school players were allowed to directly declare for the NBA draft instead of going to college. But the NBA changed the rule in its 2005 collective bargaining agreement, forcing players to be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft and one year removed from high school before they could declare.

The Realistic Fix: Let graduating high school seniors enter the draft.

There have been discussions for years about scrapping the one-and-done rule. In 2022, The Athletic's Shams Charania reported that the league and the National Basketball Players Association were "expected to agree on moving the age eligibility" from 19 to 18. However, ESPN's Adrian Wojnarowski reported in March 2023 that the two sides agreed to scrap those discussions, "clearing the way for the 'one-and-done' era to continue into the foreseeable future."

The advent of NIL rights in recent years has helped soften the blow of the one-and-done rule. The top collegiate prospects can now earn millions through sponsorship deals rather than under-the-table arrangements with boosters. As LaMelo Ball proved, top recruits can also go overseas for a year and still wind up being high lottery picks.

According to Wojnarowski, "NBA owners and executives were largely indifferent or fully against returning to high school gymnasiums to evaluate players, and even less enthusiastic about that idea without concessions from the NBPA on providing increased access to pre-draft player medical information and increased participation in several elements of the draft combine." The NBPA did ultimately make those concessions, but the one-and-done rule remained in place.

But if graduating high school seniors are ready for the NBA—as Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg proved at Team USA camp in 2024 —why should they be forced to sacrifice their NBA earning potential for a year? That only pushes back when they'll be eligible for their next contracts.

Neither the NBA nor the NBPA may feel strongly about restoring the preps-to-pros pipeline, but top high school recruits likely feel differently about it.

NBA: Bring Back Best-of-5 First-Round Series

The Problem: The logic of the seven-game series has always been bizarre: If a series is longer, the odds of an upset will decrease! And that will be better!

Is it? Why do better NBA teams need protection?

The opposite logic is what makes the NCAA tournament feel like a dozen espresso shots to the heart: less certainty is actually quite awesome!

Postseason upsets live forever. Memories of Denver over Seattle and Allan Houston over Miami keep the blood running through our veins.

Meanwhile, you've already forgotten who OKC swept in the first round last year.

So why does the NBA insist on more games, really?

More games to broadcast, more tickets to sell, more highlights to market. That's sensible logic for an owner. It's totally irrelevant to the rest of us.

The Realistic Fix: Pare things back to a best-of-five. If that's unbearable, there's also a perfectly fine compromise (h/t Bill Barnwell 12 years ago ): a mercy rule if a team goes down 3-0.

Suddenly, a 2-0 series is must-watch TV, as nobody has to suffer the inevitability of a 3-0 Game 4.

The Problem: A defender running into the path of a driving opponent at the last second, becoming a statue and then flying backward into teammates' and opponents' legs isn't safe, isn't entertaining and isn't really basketball.

The Realistic Fix: This one isn't easy, mostly because there isn't an obvious replacement for the way things are called, but the block/charge play is enough of a blight on the game that it's worth eliminating without a real alternative.

This isn't an argument to ban the offensive foul altogether. Drivers shouldn't be allowed to obviously push off, set moving screens or plow through defenders who are already in a legal guarding position. It's just a plea for defenders to stop running into an already developed play to "take" a charge instead of actually trying to defend a shot or cut the drive off.

This idea comes up often. One of the most common counters is that the offense already has too many advantages. While that may be true, if the league eliminated the block/charge play while simultaneously reining in offensive foul-baiting, the balance would be fine.

The Problem: We're tired of hearing NBA players and coaches complain about the league's extremely demanding travel obligations. We get it: Going from city to city for seven months a year must be taxing on the mind and body.

What makes the complaint a headache: The NBA was trending toward a solution as recently as five years ago, when it experimented with two-game, MLB-esque series to cut down on fraught flights. Single-game road trips were halved. It seemed like progress.

Fast-forward to 2025-26. The league kinda…forgot about this concept?

The Realistic Fix: Bring back the idea of regular-season series.

Any baseball fan will quickly tell you about all the benefits: the evolving chess moves and games within the game, the simmering tension, the glory of a sweep. The sleepovers at their rivals' houses (we assume).

Two games vs. each nonconference team become one two-game set (home one year, away the next). That's 15 sets and 30 games, with one trip per opponent instead of two.

Then conference games follow suit. Division games and other four-game opponents become two-game home-and-home sets, while teams you see three times become one two-game set with a yearly rotating one-off.

Mini two-game sets would give fans another reason to care about that early-November back-to-back that would hopefully cut down on travel-related fatigue and injuries.

The Problem: NBA games grind to a near halt in crunch time as teams intentionally foul each other. Nobody wants to watch that. Outside of a couple of fan bases (we'll leave it to you to guess which ones), no one likes watching free throws.

The Creative Fix: The Elam Ending gives us a way to bypass all of that. Instead of a timed fourth quarter, the league could add something like 28 points (around the current average for points per quarter) to the leading team's score at the end of the third quarter to give each game its "target score."

This is a more urgent fix at the lower levels of basketball (when's the last time you sat through an interminable free-throw shootout down the stretch of a high school game?), but the NBA would benefit from it too.

The sacrifice is obviously overtime, but those games can be a lot of fun. The upside is that every contest would end with a game-winner, no one would be able to run out the clock, and, most importantly, no free-throw shootouts!

The Problem: The NBA has heard your complaints. The league is addressing the tanking crisis.

Of all the major American sports leagues, its 3-2-1 lottery fix is the most progressive system.

Starting this year, teams with the three worst records will have worse odds of winning the No. 1 pick than the fourth- through 10th-worst squads.

The Creative Fix : Consider a tanking solution with high-stakes, winner-take-all drama. The proposal:

All non-playoff teams compete for lottery seeding in a postseason tournament, with the winner getting the No. 1 pick.

Tournament setup: a bracket with 14 teams, single elimination.

Play-in losers go in as seeds 11-14, no matter how they rank. (They play an extra round to disincentivize teams from tanking the play-in.)

Single games would be played mid-day, abroad, before the first round of the playoffs. Upset potential + a fast schedule + NBA games in Europe that matter.

The winner gets the No. 1 pick. Runner-up gets No. 2. Semifinal losers play for No. 3.

Quarterfinal losers enter a lottery with equal odds. First-round losers enter the same lottery with equal, worse odds.
