The Problem: Anthony Edwards has a lane to fly to the hoop for a tomahawk slam, but he stops 28 feet away and launches a three. Jaylen Brown is headed to the paint, in position to power over a 7-foot center, but he dishes out to Anfernee Simons for a corner trey.

Consider the following. In '96-97, Jerry Stackhouse had 115 dunks. In '99-00, Steve Francis had 96. But Edwards had just 48 dunks in '25-26 (4.5 percent of his shots). Brown had 32 (2.7 percent). That's a lot of spectacular that fans are no longer seeing.

Sure, off-the-dribble and logo threes can be spectacular, but way too many threes are stilted attempts on a well-spaced (read: boring) floor. Final-shot plays are usually limited to moving screens around the arc, followed by a heave. Three-and-D stiffs are prioritized over acrobats who didn't grow up with a live-in shooting coach.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: Incentivize high-wire basketball by awarding high-wire acts three points instead of two.

But wait, are we saying that Mitchell Robinson gets three points for every putback dunk he makes? No, we are not.

Using the tracking wizardry that can plot the movement of players and basketballs, a formula is set for every player, taking into account their height and their distance from the basket when they take off. Wemby's dunk from the free-throw line? Three points. Fred VanVleet's dunk from outside that little semi-circle? Three points.

In honor of Dr. J and His Airness, let's take this one to the rack.

The Problem: Threes just don't slap like they used to.

Blame Steph. Blame the math. Blame the copycats.

Ten years ago, teams averaged 24 threes attempted per game. Last year, teams averaged 37 threes per game. Everyone's just jacking . Games feel like three-point fast-break drills and the novelty of a shot from distance is gone. Yawn.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: But sources say there's a number bigger than three that could revolutionize the game, a number so bold it could make a three-pointer feel like the layup it's become: four .

Bring on the four-pointer, placed where the elite three-point specialists are already shooting from: 27 feet.

A four-point line would immediately open up the court, make end-of-game strategy fascinating and reestablish the value of the NBA's most skilled players.

All the dudes who worked on their corner three can keep chucking. But it's time to reward the heat-checkers and spice up the game flow.

The Problem: Our general POV here at Bleacher Report is simple: Superstars are fun to watch. Referees are not. Especially in college basketball.

We all watch college hoops for many reasons—the raucous student sections, the nostalgic house bands, the rivalries. But really: the stars.

So why does the NCAA insist on the antiquated five-foul limit per player? The rule comes with dire consequences for fans, removing stars when everyone wants them on the court: crunch time.

Defenders of the rule say: "(robot voice) higher foul limits lead to more fouls, more free throws and slower games. And raising the limit rewards physical play."

The Realistic Fix: Make the foul limit six.

In other words: more hoops, higher scores and lottery picks taking the game-winning shot? That's an easy trade-off for us.

The Problem: Conference realignment has run amok in recent years, which has caused longstanding college basketball rivalries to become dormant. As teams change conferences, they're no longer guaranteed to face their rivals every year.

The Realistic Fix: Every men's and women's college basketball program should designate one permanent rivalry that conference realignment can't knock off the schedule, guaranteeing a home-and-home every season.

Take Kansas and Missouri, for instance. The two teams had been facing each other since 1907 (!), but when Missouri departed the Big 12 for the SEC in 2012, the rivalry went on hiatus for nearly a decade. Luckily, cooler heads eventually prevailed to renew it , but the agreement lasts only six years and features one annual matchup, not two.

Georgetown and Syracuse are another example of a once-great rivalry that's now on pause. The Hoyas and Orange have clashed 98 times since 1930 , but their last meeting came in December 2024. They didn't meet in the 2025-26 season. They don't have a game scheduled against one another in 2026-27, either.

Conference realignment and transfer rules have made college sports feel more transient than ever before. Restoring historic rivalries—and guaranteeing a home-and-home each year instead of just one annual meeting—would go a long way toward bringing back what once made college basketball great.

The Problem: Following MLB's institution of the Automated Ball-Strike Challenge System (ABS) in 2026, teams won 53.9 percent of 10,557 challenges. That's great. But since every club gets two challenges per game and loses any that are unsuccessful, the system can only change calls while teams still have the ability. Even then, it can only do so when players call it out.

The Realistic Fix: Institute the ABS system full time. Any pitch that touches the established rectangular zone, which is 17 inches wide and stands from 53.5 percent of the batter's height at the top to 27 percent at the bottom, is a strike.

Why not do it? Well, umpires are people too, and over a century of tradition is hard to let go of. Players also prefer the challenge system to a full-on robotic takeover.

But the first time a team can't challenge an obvious blown call in a big postseason game, this issue will rear its head. There have already been instances of players failing to challenge calls that could've been overturned in key situations. MLB.com's Mike Petriello noted that both Arizona's Ketel Marte and Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio left challenges on the shelf following questionable ninth-inning called third strikes.

We have the tech. Let's get this stuff right the first time.

The Problem: MLB teams can't turn to their best hitters on demand in the biggest moments. In a world where baseball has lost its status as America's pastime, it should be able to lean on its star power the way the NBA and NFL do.

The Creative Fix: Allow teams to give one at-bat per game in the seventh inning or later to a hitter already in the lineup, no matter if it's his turn. Baseball gets its equivalent of drawing up a late-game play for its best receiver or scorer.

The inning restriction would keep the focus on tense, high-leverage decisions rather than allowing teams to use it as an opener-like strategy. Theoretically, a star player could make consecutive plate appearances, but teams would have to consider the opportunity cost of replacing their No. 4 hitter with their No. 3, for instance.

The Athletic's Jayson Stark tackled the topic as well as anyone could after MLB commissioner Rob Manfred mentioned the idea in passing in October 2024. Owners had informally discussed the golden at-bat at a competition committee meeting that year, but Manfred later said he was not in favor of the rule change. There's been nothing but silence on it since.

For the naysayers, yes, the golden at-bat flies in the face of tradition. Baseball has done plenty of that in the last half-decade or so with other rule changes such as the ghost runner. But think of the buzz in the air that rises when an ace starter comes on in relief in a short-rest playoff appearance. This would be the batter's version, as the moment would be electric.

MLB: Starting Pitchers Must Throw 60 Pitches, or Else

The Problem: The once-proud starting pitcher position is now filled by anyone who can face at least three batters, or maybe go three or four innings, and then be replaced by a parade of situational hurlers.

The bad results: There's no premium on pitchers' staying power. Fewer pitchers become the reliable foundation of a fan's experience. Pitchers are raised to throw nasty stuff at 100 mph. Then they burn out, have surgeries and float in and out of the rotation. Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby wins 13 games. Yankees starter Max Fried wins 5.

The Creative Fix: If a team chooses to pull its starting pitcher before 60 pitches, the team must also choose to either:

2) keep the SP in the game as a DH in a 10-batter lineup.

Even if you don't care about The Decline of The Starting Pitcher, you have to agree this is a great fix just for the strategic ramifications of deciding to pull a pitcher early.

MLB: Make Gold Glove Winners Wear Gold Gloves

The Problem: Who even knows about the Gold Gloves anymore? Everyone knows Greg Maddux won like a hundred of them. Maybe you've heard tell of Brooks Robinson (16 in a row), but how many of the 2026 winners are in your prize collection of baseball NFTs? Ezequiel Durán? Dillon Dingler?

Listen, fielding is important. Just ask the Playoff Yankees of late. But the hallowed MLB award for good fielding is hollow.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: No, we're not saying they have to field with a metal trophy glove, but we are saying that Gold Glove winners will play with golden gloves. Call it the Gilded Age, if that helps.

Now, when you see an All-Star like Steven Kwan take center field for the Cleveland Guardians, wearing a very shiny mitt, you'll know he's considered the AL's best center fielder, on top of his leadoff-batting skills. You'll know that his teammate Patrick Bailey might be No. 8 in the batting order, but as a catcher, he's No. 1.

If you want to extend this to the T-ball league you manage, that's cool.

The Problem: A batter saunters up to the plate as "Back in Black" pounds out of the stadium speakers. He steps to the plate and flails a meek pop-up to second base. Any air pumped into the crowd by the heavy-metal riff immediately dissipates. The very sonic value of the music is undercut by the inept hitting display. It's like displaying Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" on the bathroom wall of a one-star motel room.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: Your WAR is below 1.0. You don't get a walk-up song.

Trent Grisham made 484 regular-season plate appearances for the Yankees in 2026. His main walk-up song was Ella Langley's chart-topping "Choosin' Texas." He chose to slash .211/.308/.395 with a 0.6 WAR. No walk-up song.

One proposed alternative: Any player with a WAR below 1.0 walks up to the "Benny Hill" theme song.

One exception: Rookies get a walk-up song for their first 300 plate appearances regardless of their WAR. (But if they're not up to 1.0 WAR for PA No. 301, they trudge to the plate in silence.)

MLB: Make Fan-Caught Foul Balls Count as Outs

The Problem: Players aren't the only ones who make jaw-dropping catches. Ever seen a fan wearing a baby carrier and holding a drink manage to snag a screaming foul while the kid stays (relatively) unharmed and barely a drop of liquid hits the ground?

We need a way of crediting such athletic feats, other than with a broadcast booth chuckle and a highlight clip.

The Galaxy-Brained Fix: Award an out to the fielding team for a fan-caught foul ball on the fly. The Savannah Bananas already use this rule, but we have an added wrinkle: Fans must wear the defensive team's gear to be eligible to record an out.

While the home team would have an advantage in most cases, visitors would still have a chance. It would encourage road fans to travel well. The fan-interference rule would remain unchanged. Nobody wants the baby-strapped parent leaning into the field of play in the name of helping the team.

For everyone else? Bring your glove and get ready to live out your dreams.

The Problem: It makes little sense that the NHL awards a standings point to teams that lose in overtime or a shootout. Teams shouldn't get credit for losing.

Beyond that, clubs went from playing for ties (and a point) in OT before the league instituted the practice in 1999-00...to doing the same thing late in the third period to guarantee at least a point.

Not only does the rule not solve what it set out to fix, but it also creates situations in which teams can finish ahead of those with higher win totals, which the Sharks, Capitals and Islanders fell victim to last season. It's convoluted.

The Realistic Fix: Go back to the pre-loser-point system, with one caveat: Keep the shootout, which began in 2005-06, at the end of overtime. Teams get two points for a win, nothing for a loss and no ties.

Without the consolation point waiting, teams will have a lot less incentive to play it safe late in games. No more examples like last year's Kings, who made the playoffs with a record 20 OT or shootout losses. No more awarding losing .

NHL: Give the Awards Names Anyone Can Understand

The Problem: Art Ross, Frank J. Selke, Georges Vézina, William M. Jennings, Conn Smythe, Ted Lindsay, Frank Calder, David Hart, James E. Norris, Bill Masterton, Jack Adams, King Clancy, Maurice Richard, Roger Crozier, Mark Messier, Lady Byng of Vimy.

As everyone's favorite Canadian, Alex Trebek, might've said: Who are the NHL's awards named after?

And as every sports fan who can't skate backwards would say: What are these awards for?

We get it: Hockey kinda likes being in its own world. But it's high time for NHL Award Glasnost. We casuals who want to embrace hockey will never remember the difference between Art Ross and David Hart.

The Realistic Fix: Hart MVP, Ross Top Points Scorer, Vezina Best Goalie, Norris Defenseman of the Year, Calder Rookie of the Year, Adams Coach of the Year.

The Lady Byng, we keep. It just sounds like Best Sportsmanship.

We'd like to add The Hanson Brothers Trophy, for Best Fighter.

And the rest, you can keep as is. "Forward Who's Best at Defense" isn't much better than "the Selke Trophy."

NHL: Pull Your Goalie, You Can't Put Him Back

The Problem: Few coaching moves in any sport fire up the watchability of a game more than when a hockey coach pulls the goalie so the team can go six-on-five, trying to come back in the final minutes of a game.

It's a fun regular-season scenario and a peak postseason one: The team's down a goal with 1:30 left, but it's not hopeless. Go empty net and put another scorer on the ice! The tension rises tenfold for fans of both sides.

But then, it happens: The trailing team scores right away. The game is tied. The goalie goes back in. No more empty net. Sixty seconds of conservative play and we go to OT.

The Creative Fix: If you pull your goalie, you can't put a goalie back in the net. Go empty net with 1:30 left, your net stays empty. Score to tie the game 10 seconds later, you've still got that six-on-five advantage but you're defending an empty net for 80 seconds.

Besides doing away with the anticlimactic back-to-even-strength regulation finishes, this simple but brilliant fix adds opportunity for more final-moment goals after a tying goal.

The Problem: To put it in terms most Americans would understand, a professional soccer pitch is somewhere between a football field and the state of Kansas in square footage. Even the most well-conditioned athletes will get exhausted having to run constantly across such a large space for 90-plus minutes. This often results in some of the game's most exciting players not being part of the action in the most critical moments.

The Realistic Fix: Just let subs come back in. This is how it works in most other major team sports.

To be clear, we are not arguing for unlimited substitutions, as that would clearly have a negative effect on the game by creating too many stoppages. There are already limits to the number of substitution windows. Those should remain in place.

Apart from keeping the game moving, the only real objection to returning substitutes is that it makes stamina less a part of the game. This concern seems overblown, as needing to constantly sprint absurdly long distances still requires obscene levels of fitness. That won't change if a few key players per game are allowed to take a bit of a breather.

Giving managers the option to strategically rest players will ensure they are fresh and ready to make an impact in the most exciting moments. It will also open up entirely new options for galaxy-brained tactics that wouldn't be tenable for whole games or halves, but would be thrilling to see in a brief experiment for a few minutes.

Soccer players can and should take pride in the level of conditioning required to have made the current substitution rules viable. But let's consider their point thoroughly proven and move on to a more exciting way of managing subs.

The Problem: The range of offenses for a yellow card is so broad that it often doesn't feel like an appropriate punishment. A first yellow can sometimes feel meaningless, while a second yellow can be excessively harsh. The system needs some tinkering at the very least.

The Realistic Fix: A first yellow results in a player having to sit out for five minutes while their team plays a player down. A second yellow forces a player off for 10 minutes. A third yellow and they're off for good.

A five-minute sin bin trip solves our first problem: initial yellows are often an unsatisfactory response. This is particularly evident when a player commits a "professional foul" during a transition moment. Putting an immediate end to a dangerous counterattack robs fans of excitement. A simple yellow card is clearly not much of a deterrent considering how often this happens. Knowing that this behavior will result in an additional disadvantage will make more players think twice before that intentional shirt tug.

Then, a 10-minute penalty solves the second problem of a silly lack of judgment, totally altering a game. Yes, most second yellows can rightly be blamed on the offending player (although referees have been known to show the occasional perplexing card), even when one or both offenses are fairly innocuous. But sending off a player permanently tends to make matches less interesting. It hardly seems to violate the sanctity of the game if a player gets to continue after sitting out a significant amount of time in the wake of two less-than-egregious offenses.

This new protocol would make for fewer cynical fouls and also more matches where the competition itself, rather than an error in judgment—whether it be from a player or a ref—is the main talking point.

The Problem: Goals are fun. Stopping a game for several minutes while VAR officials show us that graphic design is their passion by drawing lines all over still frames to determine that a player's shoelace was in an offside position is not. We need fewer goals disallowed for margins that are a fraction of an inch.

The Creative Fix: Stop the madness and scrap offside beyond the 18-yard line.

The point of offside is pretty simple: prevent cherry-picking. It has to exist in some form so that players can't just spend the whole game camped out by their opponent's goal.

Getting rid of it entirely would distort the geometry of the game in absurd ways. It would make the entire field playable for the team in possession at all times, which isn't feasible given how insanely large a professional soccer pitch is. Condensing the field showcases offensive skill and defensive tenacity, making the game more exciting.

But once a team has possession near the goal, it's attacking; that rationale disappears, and so should offside. The field is already condensed. Skill and tenacity are already being displayed. Offside can only do more harm than good at this point.

To get technical—because there is no way to discuss offside in any shape or form without doing so—what we're really proposing is that offside goes away as long as both the player delivering and receiving a pass are beyond the 18-yard line. They do not actually have to be in the box.

To put it more simply: Players already in advanced attacking positions can't be offside. This would keep the game largely the same as it is now, just with fewer annoying VAR reviews and more exciting, well-deserved goals.

Soccer: Breakaways, Not Penalty Shootouts

The Problem: A penalty shootout hardly seems like a fair way to settle a match after 120 minutes of the ultimate test of endurance, skill and fortitude. It also allows a team that decided to park the bus and play for a 0-0 tie to be rewarded with a chance to advance through a contest that is largely a guessing game with a 50-50 chance of winning.

The Creative Fix: Scrap traditional spot kicks and bring back the old MLS-style breakaways.

Penalties do have one undeniable thing going for them: drama. Few things in sports deliver the tension fans and athletes feel in the moments between the ref's whistle and a player taking a spot kick. The solution to this problem has to preserve that.

While the NHL gives us a good current example of how a different format of penalties can require more skill from both the shooter and the goalie without taking the lid off the pressure cooker, we don't need to look to another sport for a better alternative. We simply need to turn the clock back to the 1990s during the formative years of Major League Soccer.

Basking in the glow of hosting the 1994 World Cup, the United States, in typical fashion, decided it was not only going to become a real soccer nation, but it was also going to make soccer better than it's ever been. It launched its latest and greatest domestic professional league. Instead of playing the game the way it's played everywhere else, efforts were made to Americanize the rules with time counting down instead of up, the clock stopping every time the ball goes out of play, and a radical new version of the penalty shootout .

Instead of traditional spot kicks, these shootouts featured a player dribbling toward goal in a simulated breakaway, needing to find a way to score while the goalie charges at them.

Thankfully, MLS has progressively moved its game more in accordance with how everyone else does it, but there is a baby in all that bathwater that was thrown out over the years. Those old-school MLS shootouts were awesome. Adopting them across the board is the lone instance where the rest of the world could take a page out of the United States' soccer notebook.

The Problem: Combat sports choose to exist on their own among professional sports by allowing championships to end in a tie. This flies in the face of what a title is supposed to be. What other sport would allow its very best to square off, then let them play to a draw and tell fans we may or may not do this all again in a few months?

The Realistic Fix: We don't need to think too hard to fix this issue. We'll just do it the way every other sport does it: overtime.

Any title fight that ends in a draw simply gets another round added to it. All boxing and UFC title fights have three ringside judges, so it is highly likely that two or more judges will favor one fighter or the other, requiring only one extra round to decide the contest.

It's theoretically possible that a judge (or three) gives a 10-10 score on the round, failing to break the deadlock. This would be a very rare occurrence. It also has a simple solution. Trot the fighters back out for yet another round until we have a decisive score from the judges.

Besides removing the possibility of such an unsatisfactory ending to a title fight, this change would also produce some incredible drama during these new overtime rounds.

The Problem: Any major combat sports event is going to promise plenty of action, but inevitably some will fail to deliver. Hardcore MMA fans will admirably wax poetic on the nuances of technique and strategy, but the mainstream lifeblood of the sport is big blows landing to produce thrilling highlights. Why not tilt the playing field to make more of these moments?

The Realistic Fix: Move the walls in a few feet, similar in size to the UFC's Apex cage, giving less space for the biggest, baddest, strongest fighters to escape each other. With the action forced right into the middle of the Octagon, fans will know that a heavyweight fight is going to deliver.

Limiting this to just the giants is a nice compromise between the hardcore and casual fans. The former still gets to see most of the fights on any given card carry on in the traditional way. The latter gets more action and knockouts for one or two select bouts.

Changing the physical infrastructure of the Octagon mid-card may seem impractical, but the folks at modern-day sports venues have proven themselves to be miracle workers. Arenas commonly switch from a hockey rink to a basketball court on the same day. We just saw crews figure out how to install natural grass in domed stadiums for the World Cup. And WWE shows deliver all sorts of stunts involving cages appearing in the middle of a show.

It may not be easy, but there's little doubt it's entirely possible. And not only would it produce more exciting fights, but the process would be dramatic in its own right. Seeing the walls literally close in would build incredible tension ahead of a heavyweight showdown.

Boxing, MMA: Show the Scorecards After Every Round

The Problem: Combat sports once again stand alone in not allowing fans to know the score while the contest is happening. Even beyond your typical stick-and-ball sports, other contests involving rounds and judges like gymnastics or various extreme sports still show official judges' marks along the way, while boxing and MMA fans are left relying on a commentator's guess at what the score is at any given time.

The Realistic Fix: It couldn't be simpler. Judges are already writing down and submitting their scores after every round. Show those on the broadcast, and let the fighters know what they are.

The common argument against doing this is it will incentivize a fighter who knows they're in the lead to take a defensive posture and produce less exciting fights. This logic cuts both ways, though. A fighter who knows they're down is going to sell out on trying to land big blows.

Our take is any strategic changes that result from fighters knowing the score during fights would at worst balance out between incentivizing more offensive or defensive tactics. And in all likelihood, it'll produce more exciting moments, as we'll more often get to see the combat equivalent of a Hail Mary when fighters know for sure they're down rather than having to guess that's the case.

This change—which has already been experimented with over recent years—will bring more entertainment to the fans, more transparency and accountability from the judges, and make everyone more informed about what's going on along the way. Unlike the actual fights, everyone wins here.

The Problem: When a serve ticks the net and lands in, it's a "let." Try again. The problems here are myriad.

First, it's hardly fair that if a serve ticks the net cord and lands out , it's out, but if it lands in, it's a do-over.

Third, there can be dispute over whether or not it was a let, seeing as the chair umpire has to detect it and call it.

Fourth, two great servers can make for a pretty boring match, so it'd be good to get some luck involved.

Fifth, it's always been super-confusing that when the ball ticks the "net," it's a "let."

The Realistic Fix: No service lets. If the ball hits the net cord and lands in, it's in. Play on!

(This is actually the rule in NCAA tennis, by the way, so we're not being crazy.)

With this easy fix we fix all five problems.

And now we're going to get points where the serve pops up and the returner crushes it. Or the ball just gets over and the returner dashes for it. Maybe some players perfect serving off the net cord!

And no more of this "net," "let" business.

Tennis: Make All Matches Best-of-3 (Except Men's and Women's Finals)

The Problem: Best-of-five singles matches frequently are too long.

Too long for TV viewers. Too long for spectators. Too long for maintaining a reasonable match schedule at majors for the players and tournament staff. Made longer by cramping timeouts and multiple shirt changes. Too long.

Just the specter of how long they could be mars the fan experience.

One related problem: In best-of-five, a player down two service breaks in an early set often mails in the rest of the set, so he can save energy for the next set. Watching a guy go through the motions from 0-3 to 1-6 is not what we need.

The Creative Fix: Make all matches best-of-three no matter the magnitude of the tournament, except for the major finals—men's and women's—which will be best-of-five.

Now, when you settle in to watch a match, you won't have to worry that the first hour or two will be ultimately meaningless. Now, if someone wins the opening set with authority, it will really mean something toward the ultimate result.

A side benefit of this fix is that it will prevent another "fix" some people suggest: Making all women's matches best-of-five at the majors. Not that many, many fans wouldn't rather watch five-set women's matches than five-set men's matches, but we really should avoid an evolution to both sexes playing best-of-five, because then the U.S. Open would be a full month of 2 a.m. finishes.

articles.title: 6 Trade Landing Spots for Matvei Michkov Amid NHL Rumors
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Flyers are just 20 games into the season, and they've already had a full season's worth of intrigue. Worse yet, they've had a good chunk of that happen over the past couple of days thanks to Matvei Michkov.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Flyers are just 20 games into the season, and they've already had a full season's worth of intrigue. Worse yet, they've had a good chunk of that happen over the past couple of days thanks to Matvei Michkov.

It started with Michkov and teammate Nick Seeler shouting at each other on the bench during the Flyers' win against Vancouver on Monday night. That was followed on Tuesday by a report from ESPN's Kevin Weekes that Michkov, currently in the last year of his entry-level contract, is ready to move on from Philly.

While Weekes noted that Michkov wants to go, ESPN's Emily Kaplan reported that he has not formally requested a trade and the report itself was news to the Flyers' front office.

Michkov has shown flashes of brilliance in his two-plus NHL seasons, and he's off to a strong offensive start this season. He leads the Flyers with 10 goals and is tied with Trevor Zegras for the team lead with 14 points. However, his minus-11 rating is the lowest on the team.

It's the duality of being an offense-first player, and his focus on playing high-end offensively has led to him losing ice time for various head coaches, including Rick Tocchet.

If Michkov does indeed want to go elsewhere, there would assuredly be teams lining up to have him score goals for them. We're here to pick out who among them would be most interesting.

Flash back to the 2023 NHL Draft when Matvei Michkov went seventh overall to Philadelphia. As much as that wasn't a surprise, what was a bit stunning was that the Montréal Canadiens didn't take him fifth overall despite heavy rumormongering saying they wanted him. Fast-forward three years, and the potential for Michkov to land with the Canadiens may be renewed.

The Canadiens are aggressive on the trade market, always, and if Michkov wanted to go to the Habs, he'd have a familiar face in Ivan Demidov there to greet him, as they were once teammates in Russia. With the high pace and breakneck offensive style the Canadiens play with, Michkov would be a natural fit there.

Montréal has the assets to make any number of trades happen, and they have the assets to entice Philadelphia if Michkov, indeed, is looking for a new team to play for. With how good the Canadiens have been this season, seeing them add to their roster to get even better would deliver a firm message to the East that they're all-in.

One reason we like Mammoth GM Bill Armstrong is that he's never afraid to make a move to improve the team when he sees the opportunity.

He did it a couple of years ago at the draft when he added Mikhail Sergachev and John Marino, and he did it again in free agency this year when he added Anders Lee to a team that needed a solid veteran presence up front.

With Matvei Michkov maybe looking for a new address, Utah is a team that makes a lot of sense.

The Mammoth have a couple of younger Russian players in Daniil But and Dmitri Simashev, and adding Michkov with them would make sense from a chemistry standpoint. Utah also already has a load of younger players at the top of their game in Logan Cooley and Dylan Guenther, with more on the way with Caleb Desnoyers, Tij Iginla, and 2026 first-rounder Ethan Belchetz.

Would they part with one of those guys to add Michkov? Philly would probably love to add Desnoyers to their own group of prospects.

If Matvei Michkov does indeed want to make a move out of Philadelphia, the Flyers might be able to make a simple enough trade with Detroit that can take care of a couple of teams' problems at once.

The Red Wings have yet to agree to a contract with defenseman Simon Edvinsson, who reportedly wants a trade amid the impasse. A one-for-one swap for Michkov could address needs for both Detroit and Philadelphia.

The Flyers would add size and depth to their blue line with Edvinsson, while the Red Wings would gain another offensive weapon as they prepare for a potential future without Dylan Larkin. Michkov wouldn't fill the void at center, but Detroit needs scoring help wherever it can find it.

A deal like this likely wouldn't be so straightforward, but it could give both teams a starting point for trade talks.

The Flames and Flyers have had enough connections in recent years, making deals that involved younger players who suddenly weren't in Philly's plans anymore. Morgan Frost and Joel Farabee landed in Calgary after they wound up in former coach John Tortorella's doghouse. If Matvei Michkov wanted to go and the Flames wanted to have him, a deal could be put together quickly.

Calgary has other young players and prospects to interest the Flyers if that's what they were seeking in return. The Flames would certainly love to add more scoring, and a younger player like Michkov would fit their plan.

Guys like Cole Reschny, Cullen Potter, or Jack Hextall wouldn't be NHL-ready for a couple of years, but they'd help add to the Flyers' pipeline. There are other young players currently in the Flames lineup as well, but with how sudden all of this is with Michkov, piecing together what the Flyers would want is part of the equation that's a bit of a mystery.

This one is a bit of a stretch idea for us, given how well things are going for the Minnesota Wild, but Matvei Michkov would make for a really interesting fit for them for some obvious reasons.

Yes, Michkov has a lot of offensive ability, but the Wild also have a host of fellow Russians for him to fit in with rather easily. Kirill Kaprizov, Maxim Shabanov and Danila Yurov have done well together there offensively, and Yakov Trenin has been a physical force lower in the lineup.

One wrinkle is that Yurov has already surfaced in trade rumors involving Dylan Larkin. We're not suggesting the Wild should offer him for Michkov, especially with another full season remaining on his entry-level contract after this one.

Still, the chance for Michkov to play alongside fellow Russians is worth considering, given Minnesota's success with Russian players.

It would be a bit odd for the Flyers to trade their top young player to the Carolina Hurricanes, who eliminated Philadelphia from last season's playoffs before winning the Stanley Cup. Still, that divisional rivalry might not stop Hurricanes GM Eric Tulsky from pursuing a deal.

Carolina has had success with Russian players such as Andrei Svechnikov, Pyotr Kochetkov and Alexander Nikishin. Adding Matvei Michkov as a potential long-term offensive threat would be appealing to the Hurricanes—and the prospect of facing him regularly for years to come would likely give the Flyers pause.

Still, Carolina has players and prospects to offer and a savvy GM capable of putting a deal together. But Flyers GM Danny Brière would likely prefer to keep Michkov rather than trade him—especially to a division rival.

articles.title: NHL Power Rankings: Red-Hot Devils, Bruins Shoot Up This Week
articles.summary: Some teams are reveling in November. Others, not so much.
articles.body:
Some teams are reveling in November. Others, not so much.

No fewer than six teams started the week on win streaks of at least three games, while four others had dropped at least three straight by Monday's end.

Not surprisingly, the scalding hot New Jersey Devils crashed the top five in the latest edition of B/R's NHL Power Rankings, amid a prolonged run toward the top of the Metropolitan Division, which is now the domain of the Carolina Hurricanes.

B/R's hockey staff got together to vote (awarding 32 points for a first-place vote all the way down to one point for a No. 32 tally), and the point totals created the 32-to-1 ranking that follows.

Take a look at what we came up with and drop a thought in the app comments.

Statistics updated through games of Monday, Nov. 9.

ANA | BOS | BUF | CAR | CBJ | CGY | CHI | COL | DAL | DET | EDM | FLA | LAK | MIN | MTL | NJD | NSH | NYI | NYR | OTT | PHI | PIT | SEA | SJS | STL | TBL | TOR | UTA | VAN | VGK | WPG | WSH

The plummet continues for the Canucks, whose home loss to Philadelphia was their sixth straight and left them two points behind Chicago in the NHL basement. Vancouver was 32nd overall in 2025-26, 14 points behind the Blackhawks.

It went from bad to worse for the skidding Blackhawks in Carolina, where they gave up nine goals in a sixth consecutive loss. Chicago has allowed 31 regulation goals in the half-dozen losses and its 4.22 goals-against average is 31st in the NHL.

A win in Vancouver came at the right time for the Flyers, who'd lost the first two on a five-game trip and still had to visit Edmonton and Columbus before they were back home on Sunday. Philadelphia's 23 road wins were seventh in the NHL in 2025-26.

The bigger issue for Philly? Matvei Michkov may want out . Bad times in the City of Brotherly Love.

The Most Devastating NHL Injuries So Far 😭

Re-Ranking the Top 2027 NHL Free Agents 📊

A three-game jaunt to California began with a win at Los Angeles that ended a four-game skid for the Penguins, but turned ugly with a three-goal loss in Anaheim. The trip ends with a game in San Jose before a home game on Saturday.

A win over the New York Islanders was San Jose's first after five losses and just its second in nine games. "Good to get two points, right?" coach Ryan Warsofsky said . "Obviously, haven't got one here in a little bit, so that's a big thing."

Loose play with the puck led to goals against and the Kings never recovered in a loss to visiting Pittsburgh. "It usually leads to opposition and possible runs coming back at you," coach Peter Laviolette said , "possible goals coming back at you."

A loss at Buffalo was bad because it ended a two-game Columbus win streak. But it was worse because it left players questioning effort. "They were noticeably hungrier, which it hurts to say. That shouldn't be," forward Charlie Coyle said .

Losses in the final three games of a four-game road trip left frustrated coach Jim Montgomery longing for full-time effort. "We need to be more committed to who we are," he said , "and we need to work at a harder rate more consistently."

The Flames welcomed Devin Cooley back to the crease for a win against Philadelphia after a lower-body injury. Cooley has won the last five games he's started and finished, allowing nine goals on 168 shots (a .946 save percentage).

A nine-game skid (0-7-2) certainly didn't help matters, but the three straight wins that followed were a product of leadership, coach Scott Arniel said . "Our guys in our room have done a really good job of kind of keeping the noise away," he said.

Not handling adversity was troublesome for the Red Wings in a 4-0 loss at Colorado, in which Detroit had 13 first-period shots. "It was frustrating," coach Todd McLellan said , "and we didn't deal real well with our emotions."

Gavin McKenna had the full rookie experience against Montreal, scoring his sixth goal and riding the bench for a bit after a turnover on a cross-ice pass led directly to a Canadiens goal. "I knew I was going to probably sit for that one," he said .

The Rangers outshot and outplayed Edmonton over 60 minutes but saw a three-game win streak end with a second loss to the Oilers in eight days. "I loved our game," coach Mike Sullivan said . "We controlled a lot of play. There was so much to like."

A shootout loss to San Jose wasn't an ideal way to start a trip for the Islanders, who've not won in four games (0-2-2). "I don't know about the last four games," coach Peter DeBoer said . "We were better for stretches, but not long enough."

The final stretch before a trip to Europe for the NHL's Global Series in Finland didn't go so well for the Kraken, who lost two of three. Seattle will face Carolina at Veikkaus Arena in Helsinki on Thursday and Saturday.

The Panthers finished seventh in an eight-team Atlantic Division that had four 100-point teams last season, and they're off to a slow start against that competition in 2026-27 after a loss in Boston plunged them to 0-4 in the Atlantic.

A stretch of four wins in five games was halted by a home loss to Vegas, which Tage Thompson said was due to fundamentals. "Trying to get too cute at the line," he said , "giving them free offense and then we're chasing the game."

One stop remains (in Vegas) on a six-game road trip that has seen the Mammoth amass five of a possible 10 points. They opened with two wins in the trip's first three games but were subsequently beaten in Montreal (5-4) and Ottawa (4-2).

No one's hotter out West than Cutter Gauthier and the Ducks, who've won five in a row. The 22-year-old winger has scored 13 goals during a six-game goal streak. "I'm just shooting the puck and they're going in," he said , "so I'm just going to keep shooting it."

A two-game home skid in which the Capitals allowed 11 goals ended with a defeat of Florida. "To just fight through a little bit of adversity (Saturday), gut that out as a group, against a really good team," coach Spencer Carbery said , "that's a big win."

The Senators have been finding ways to win, and coach Travis Green saw their home victory over Utah as another encouraging sign. "I thought in ways it was our best win of the year," he said . "We found a way to win a game that we didn't play our best."

It's been rough for Steven Stamkos since he arrived in Nashville but early success this season may be changing the mindset. "(Confidence) is hard to get and easy to lose sometimes," he said . "When you have it, you just try to keep that snowball rolling."

Mackenzie Blackwood hasn't allowed more than three goals in a game since early October but he finally got a 2026-27 shutout when he stopped 27 shots against Detroit. "Whenever you can come away with zero," he said , "it's a good feeling."

The league's No. 7 power play (27.5 percent) thrived against San Jose, thanks largely to Thomas Harley's goal and two assists while up a man. "We're snapping it around pretty quick," he said . "I'm trying to distribute, but also be a shot threat."

The Golden Knights picked up points in each game of an eastern trip and extended a win streak to three at Buffalo. "It was a great road trip," said Tomas Hertl, who scored twice against the Sabres. "We got almost every point except one."

A loss at Winnipeg ended a six-game point streak (4-0-2) for the Lightning, though they did rally from three goals down in the third period less than 24 hours after winning in OT at Minnesota. "We were a gassed group," coach Jon Cooper said .

Jacob Fowler is just 21 but he's already in the milestone business. The rookie's win over Toronto made him the first 21-or-younger goalie with a nine-game point streak (8-0-1) since Braden Holtby did it with Washington in 2010-11.

Getting three points on a weekend back-to-back (win over San Jose, OT loss to Tampa Bay) was enough to generate positive feedback from coach John Hynes. "I liked our compete level and how we worked and things like that," he said .

No Eastern team was any hotter to start the week than the Devils, who saw the recently acquired Connor Hellebuyck become the first goalie in franchise history to win his first five games. "It's almost been a seamless transition," he said .

Devon Levi was dinged up at the end of October and the beginning of November, but his return has meant good things for the Oilers. He stopped 49 of 52 shots (.942 save percentage) in consecutive defeats of Vancouver and the Rangers.

The Bruins have been difficult to beat regardless of location so far in 2026-27 but it's been nearly impossible in Boston, where the team's Sunday defeat of Florida lifted it to 8-1-0 at home. Boston's 29 home wins last season were first in the NHL.

The Hurricanes were already limiting chances and winning games, but the floodgates opened offensively when they scored nine times in a home win against Chicago. "That's a product of coming ready to play," coach Rod Brind'Amour said .

articles.title: Drew McIntyre and 6 WWE Stars Who Could Make a Shocking Return at Survivor Series: WarGames
articles.summary: Although WWE premium live events in 2026 have largely lacked must-see moments, Survivor Series: WarGames has a chance to break the trend.
articles.body:
Although WWE premium live events in 2026 have largely lacked must-see moments, Survivor Series: WarGames has a chance to break the trend.

The men's WarGames match alone, which will see The Bloodline battle The 946, has the potential to be the best one since WWE brought the concept to the main roster in 2022. The expected women's WarGames bout has less of a reason to exist but could still have a surprise in store.

The card has barely begun to take shape in the wake of Crown Jewel 2026, but Becky Lynch vs. Liv Morgan for the Women's World Championship has already been announced. It's entirely possible a familiar face in the title scene resurfaces to factor into the finish.

The November classic has been known to feature its fair share of iconic debuts throughout its illustrious history, with The Undertaker, The Rock, The Shield and Sting all making their first-ever WWE appearances at the event.

A slew of shocking returns could transpire at this year's installment of Survivor Series: WarGames, and these seven Superstars are among the most likely to return.

Drew McIntyre was a pretty important fixture on SmackDown in the first few months of the year, first as Undisputed WWE champion and then as Jacob Fatu's archrival. The two settled their score in an Unsanctioned match at WrestleMania 42 where Fatu won decisively.

The Scottish Warrior hasn't been seen since, at least not on WWE TV.

He's been busy making a name for himself in Hollywood and honing his craft as an actor. However, a return to the squared circle is inevitable, and there's no better time for him to pop up again than at Survivor Series.

Although McIntyre was a member of the blue brand up until his hiatus, it'd make more sense for him to make the move over to Monday nights upon his return. He has unfinished business with The Bloodline, and thus it'd make sense for him to attempt to cost them a win in WarGames at Survivor Series.

From there, he can firmly set his sights on Reigns' World Heavyweight Championship.

Despite the abundance of female talent on SmackDown currently, Rhea Ripley's absence has certainly been felt the last six months.

She walked out of WrestleMania 42 the new WWE women's champion and even successfully defended the title in a rematch against Jade Cargill at Clash in Italy, but a torn meniscus in her right knee has kept her out of action ever since.

Initially, an interim champion was set to be crowned at SummerSlam, but once it became clear that Ripley wouldn't be back for the foreseeable future, Chelsea Green (by virtue of her victory at the event) would be declared the actual champ instead.

If for some reason her road to recovery has been accelerated and she's secretly been cleared to compete, then she'd be a logical addition to the babyface team for women's WarGames at Survivor Series. She's no stranger to competing inside the double cage and has history with Cargill as well as Fatal Influence.

If she returns and helps her team win WarGames, she could gradually transition back into the championship picture.

Rhea Ripley being back for WarGames is far from a guarantee, so with the babyface team needing at least one or two women to fill out their team against Jade Cargill, her "baddies" and Fatal Influence, they may need to look to other options.

There aren't a ton of women on SmackDown or Raw right now who would make sense for the spot. Most people would be considered underwhelming, but not if they call upon AJ Lee for some assistance.

Lee last competed at WrestleMania 42, where she lost the Women's Intercontinental Championship back to Becky Lynch. She ended her post-WrestleMania 42 social media address with "see you soon," implying that the audience hasn't seen the last of her on WWE TV.

Needless to say, she has no existing issue with either of the heel factions, but neither did Bayley prior to last week. Lee being recruited can easily be explained as Bayley bringing in an old friend to help her even the odds.

WWE did something similar with Lee last year in WarGames and she ultimately emerged victorious by tapping out Lynch. This could be how her next run begins, and perhaps she'll make some new enemies along the way.

Survivor Series Match Card Predictions 🔮

In classic LA Knight fashion, he narrowly fell short of winning the World Heavyweight Championship at Money in the Bank despite having the entire New Orleans crowd that night and all of the momentum in the world on his side.

Regardless of whether he will ultimately win "the big one" or not, fans were left with the question of what's next for him in WWE coming off his latest loss. His appearance on the subsequent Raw was kept brief, as he was confronted backstage by Solo Sikoa and mentioned Sikoa being back in the good graces of The Bloodline.

Knight assured Sikoa that they were still on the same page, but his tone and mannerisms indicated the exact opposite. There was a possibility of WWE adding Knight to The 946's WarGames team (not necessarily to the faction itself), but Cruz Montana has since joined the heel stable and will fill out their five-man squad.

Much like Drew McIntyre, Knight has a bone to pick with The Bloodline (specifically Sikoa) and could be the reason why they lose at Survivor Series. It'd not only give Knight some direction coming out of the show but would also effectively turn him heel for the first time in over three years.

If Knight won't be winning a world title anytime soon (if ever), he should at least be kept in the main event mix and this would accomplish that.

Stephanie Vaquer having to take time off at various points throughout 2026 has prevented her from reaching the level of stardom she found herself at a year ago when she first won the Women's World Championship.

It was a breath of fresh air to have her back in the title hunt post-SummerSlam and then for her to regain the gold in her home country of Chile at a non-televised event in September, but her reign was sadly short-lived. She lost the belt back to Liv Morgan mere weeks later at Money in the Bank, and was deemed unable to compete a few weeks later ahead of a scheduled match with Becky Lynch on Raw.

There's no exact timetable for her return, but it could be as soon as Survivor Series if what she's currently dealing with isn't too serious.

As opposed to putting her in the women's WarGames match a la Rhea Ripley or AJ Lee, it'd be best for her to make her presence felt either during or after the Women's World title bout between Morgan and Lynch.

Vaquer vs. Morgan has been done to death, but there is a story worth telling with her and Lynch, so Vaquer getting into it with The Man whether she wins the title or not would reignite their rivalry and keep both of them busy through the end of the year and beyond.

The rise of The 946 on Raw and specifically the introduction of Jaida Parker has led to rumblings in recent months of Naomi returning imminently and siding with The Bloodline to counteract her involvement.

Naomi has been married to Jimmy Uso since 2014, though the two haven't been an on-screen unit in over a decade. Embarking on separate paths has allowed them to find their own success, but in light of the current circumstances, she should be backing up The Bloodline in WarGames.

She won't be in WarGames itself this year as the match is already confirmed to be five-on-five with the men, but she could simply show up and ensure Parker does not lend a helping hand to The 946. A program with Naomi would put Parker in a prime position to shine as a singles star.

Naomi was enjoying one of the best runs of her career when she relinquished the Women's World Championship after announcing her pregnancy in the summer of 2025. Having given birth in March, she could make her return at Survivor Series, a stage befitting her long-awaited comeback.

The time will come for her to chase after the championship she never lost, but first, she can add to the excitement surrounding the men's WarGames match this year by resurfacing at Survivor Series and give Parker her comeuppance.

Seth Rollins has been radio silent on WWE TV since suffering defeat at the hands of Roman Reigns at SummerSlam, ending a 14-year story between the two.

It was an ideal time for Rollins to disappear for a bit and freshen up his character, but he should be due back any day now.

It seems to be more of a creative call to keep him off television than it is anything injury-related. There's no shortage of fresh faces for him to work with on Raw, so WWE should be looking to get him in the fold again by the end of the year.

Since it was at Survivor Series where he debuted alongside the rest of The Shield in 2012, it'd be fitting for him to make his highly anticipated return at this year's installment, potentially as the final member of Team USA against Team Mexico.

The U.S. team currently consists of Cody Rhodes, CM Punk and Je'Von Evans, and adding another A-lister in Rollins would make them virtually unstoppable. They can set up his next storyline with whoever is responsible for eliminating him as well.

While it wouldn't be as shocking as some of the aforementioned names, the return of Rollins would be a welcome boost to Survivor Series and the Raw roster in general.

articles.title: England wheelchair rugby league: World Cup bid being driven by two brothers
articles.summary: England's bid to retain the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup on Friday will be driven by two brothers - one of whom is the head coach, the other a player.
articles.body:
"It's the hardest thing that I've ever done from a work perspective," Tom Coyd said, "but also the most rewarding".

Coyd is discussing the unusual challenge he faces as head coach of England's wheelchair rugby league team - he has to manage his younger brother Joe.

By their own admission, the family dynamic can make for some tense moments.

But it worked four years ago as England won the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup. And on Friday, they hope to win the trophy again by beating great rivals France in the final in Wollongong, Australia (08:45 GMT).

"It's taught me loads about how to be a good brother and loads about how to be a good coach," said Tom, who has been England head coach since 2020. "Hopefully Joe agrees. But it is an interesting dynamic.

"I think there's a reason it doesn't happen very often because it can be really difficult. But in our quirky ways, Joe and I find a way to make it function.

"So it can be something that is a bit strange, but we make it work. And I think the team gets a lot out of it when we do get it right."

Joe was part of the England set-up before his older brother, playing at the 2013 World Cup as a 15-year-old, and now taking part in his fourth tournament.

He has been a key figure in England's run to the final - scoring in every game as they have beaten Wales, the USA, Ireland and Australia - and earning a spot on the eight-strong shortlist in the wheelchair category for the International Rugby League (IRL) Golden Boot award.

"I know I'm in a very lucky and privileged place to to be able to do the things that we get to do alongside my family," Joe said.

"When we don't get it right, it's just because we care, and we've probably got that familiarity with each other, where sometimes we're probably a bit shorter with each other.

"We might say things differently to how I might say them to one of the team-mates or another member of staff because I've grown up alongside Tom.

"But it's great. It's so cool to do it. I don't know another place where we get this opportunity, so we do our best to make the most of it."

Wheelchair rugby league runs through the Coyd family: Father Martin was an England international, played a significant role in the sport's development, and is now the team's general manager as well as a member of the Rugby Football League board.

"He's been out here busy fulfilling his responsibilities as a RFL board member," Tom said.

"But he's been doing that alongside getting oily and repairing wheelchair parts and getting his hands dirty. So he's been in the thick of it and he wouldn't have it any other way.

"I think all of the kind of peaks and troughs that come with competition, he tends to ride those waves very steadily.

"And as someone who's been at the head of the team for over a decade, he sets the standard and drives the culture. He does a good job for us."

World Cup finalists England still feel short of best

How Hawkins overcame illness to star for England

Chair skills, quick brain - how O'Neill adapted to wheelchair rugby league

Friday's match will be the fourth successive Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup final to be contested between England and France.

The previous three finals have all been tight - France triumphed 42-40 in Gillingham in 2013, and 38-34 in Perpignan in 2017, before England clinched a dramatic 28-24 win in Manchester four years ago.

"That's World Cup and Test match football, isn't it?" Joe said. "And France have been one of the leaders of the game internationally since it began. Every time we play them it's a great contest."

Joe features as one of England's non-disabled players - two of whom are allowed per five-strong team on court at any one time under wheelchair rugby league rules.

They will take on a France side who have also won all four of their matches on the way to the final - defeating Scotland, New Zealand, Australia and Ireland.

Their most experienced player is captain Gilles Clausells, a scorer in the 82-26 semi-final win over Ireland at the age of 63, and still playing despite having vowed to retire after each of the past two World Cups.

"We know how hungry they are and we know how hungry we are," Joe said. "So I've got no doubt it's going to be an amazing clash on Friday. And both teams will be up for it."

Coyd and Hawkins on Golden Boot shortlist

Joe Coyd and his England team-mate Rob Hawkins both made the shortlist in the wheelchair category for the IRL Golden Boot award - given to the world's best rugby league player over the calendar year.

"I'm so proud of Rob and Joe for being acknowledged, and they've spoken about how it's their team-mates that have got them there, as you'd expect," Tom said.

"They're humble characters and that's what got them in this position. But yeah, I think they've both had fantastic tournaments and they've worked incredibly hard."

Australia full-back Reece Walsh and his New Zealand counterpart Kalyn Ponga are both in contention for the men's award. New Zealand centre Stacey Waaka - scorer of a hat-trick in their 32-0 semi-final win over Samoa - is up for the women's award. Other contenders include Australia winger Abbi Church, who replaced the injured Julia Robinson to score four times in their 30-14 semi-final win over Fiji.

The winners of all three awards will be announced in Brisbane on Thursday.

articles.title: Mbappe misses France training before Nations League clash with Italy
articles.summary: Kylian Mbappe left the pitch during France’s game in September but has been playing regularly for Real Madrid.
articles.body:
France captain Kylian Mbappe has not taken part in team training and remains “under treatment” before his country’s Nations League clash with Italy, the Les Bleus coaching staff says.

It did not provide any details regarding the 27-year-old’s physical condition after Wednesday’s training session.

The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad after missing their last three matches through injury .

Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zinedine Zidane’s first match as coach against Turkiye in September in the Nations League but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee .

Shortly before this international break, the Frenchman scored in Real’s 3-0 away win over Valencia in La Liga on Saturday. Mbappe is the second-highest scorer in the Spanish top flight this term with 13 goals, two fewer than leader Raphinha of Barcelona.

After three wins and a draw in four matches, two-time world champions France top Group A1 of the Nations League and are well on course to qualify for the quarterfinals before their final two pool-stage fixtures against Italy on Thursday in Milan and Turkiye on Sunday in Bordeaux.

articles.title: Ranking the 5 Greatest WWE Survivor Series 5-on-5 Tag Team Matches Ever
articles.summary: The traditional 5-on-5 elimination tag team match will return to Survivor Series on November 28, when Cody Rhodes leads Team USA against Rey Mysterio's Team Mexico.
articles.body:
The traditional 5-on-5 elimination tag team match will return to Survivor Series on November 28, when Cody Rhodes leads Team USA against Rey Mysterio's Team Mexico.

With CM Punk and Je'Von Evans already pledging to compete for the U.S. squad and Penta siding with Mysterio, the talent level promises to be off the charts. Will it live up to the standard set by the best versions of that staple match?

Time will tell. Until then, relive the best 5-on-5 elimination bouts from the 39-year history of Survivor Series, ranked based on overall quality, storyline strength and historic significance.

Strike Force, British Bulldogs, Killer Bees, The Rougeaus, and The Young Stallions vs. The Hart Foundation, Demolition, The Bolsheviks, The Islanders, and The Dream Team (1987)

If you are looking for an indicator of just how strong tag team wrestling was in 1987 WWE, look no further than the inaugural Survivor Series, which featured 10 tag teams in one match. Not quite the traditional 5-on-5, and thus not worthy of inclusion on the list. Still, this was a damn good match with some of the best workers in company history sharing the ring at the same time.

Marty Jannetty, Hakushi, Barry Horowitz, and Bob Holly vs. The 1-2-3 Kid, Dr. Tom Prichard, Rad Radford and Skip (1995)

Strictly looking at this who's who of WrestleCrap infamy would not necessarily inspire fans to track it down, but this match from the highly underrated 1995 show features some great action from young and veteran talent alike, including a top-rope powerbomb from Jannetty to Skip that was otherworldly in WWE at the time.

Triple H, Shawn Michaels, The Hardy Boyz, and CM Punk vs. Edge, Randy Orton, Mike Knox, Gregory Helms, and Johnny Nitro (2006)

Not a particularly great match, this 2006 contest was as notable for the enormous reaction given to CM Punk—even while he shared the ring with the legendary D-Generation X and Hardy Boyz—as it was for anything that happened between the bells. The babyfaces' dominance, Michaels having zero clue who Knox was, and a red-hot Philadelphia crowd elevate this one, even if it is too one-sided to be much more than an enjoyable rout.

Hulk Hogan vs. Andre the Giant was such a profitable match-up that WWE and Vince McMahon quite literally created a new pay-per-view event in November of 1987 to capitalize on the popularity of that rivalry.

In the main event of the inaugural show, Hogan captained a team consisting of "Mr. Wonderful" Paul Orndorff, Don Muraco, Ken Patera, and Bam Bam Bigelow against Andre, King Kong Bundy, "Ravishing" Rick Rude, "The Natural" Butch Reed, and One Man Gang.

In a moment of utter unpredictability, Hogan was eliminated when he was counted out, the culmination of a scheme concocted by the heels. With his team captain out of the equation, Bigelow took center stage and delivered a star-making performance, pinning Gang and Bundy before succumbing to the giant.

An expertly laid out match, featuring six Hall of Famers and four others who should be, it was the perfect capper to a historic night that would set the stage for every traditional Survivor Series Elimination Tag Team Match that would follow.

It was with a renewed focus on the brand split, and both Raw and SmackDown establishing their own identities, that an interpromotional battle took to the squared circle at the 2016 Survivor Series.

Roman Reigns, Seth Rollins, Chris Jericho, Kevin Owens, and Braun Strowman represented the red brand against SmackDown's Dean Ambrose, Bray Wyatt, Randy Orton, AJ Styles, and Shane McMahon.

What set the match apart from others is that it was not simply 10 wrestlers having a great match built on dramatic near-falls, cool spots, and shocking eliminations.

It also featured the intertwining of several ongoing storylines, including the highly entertaining friendship between Jericho and Owens, the tension between Styles and McMahon, and the union of Orton and Wyatt.

Throw in the prodigal son's soul getting speared out of his body by Reigns, and a mid-match Shield reunion that saw Ambrose join The Big Dog and Rollins for a triple powerbomb to Styles, and you had a match that evolved and reinvigorated what had become somewhat of a tired staple.

Survivor Series Match Card Predictions 🔮

The evil, power-drunk Authority, led by Triple H and Stephanie McMahon, made life a living hell for any Superstars who opposed them.

At the 2014 event, they led a team captained by Seth Rollins and featuring Kane, Luke Harper, Mark Henry, and Rusev into battle against John Cena, Ryback, Big Show, Erick Rowan, and Dolph Ziggler.

A win by the heels would cost Cena's four teammates their jobs. A victory for the heroes would strip The Authority of power.

What ensued was a high-drama affair that saw Big Show shockingly betray Cena, allowing Rollins to pin the biggest star in the company and leave the fate of the babyfaces in Ziggler's hands.

Ziggler had always been tremendously talented, but he had rarely been presented as a world-beater. With the match resting on his shoulders, termination appeared imminent for Cena's remaining allies.

Down to the resilient babyface and Rollins, pressure set in for Triple H and Stephanie McMahon. The former laid out referees and dropped Ziggler with the Pedigree, only for the great avenger, Sting, to finally make his WWE debut. He laid out The Game, put Ziggler on top of Rollins, then watched as the underdog scored one of the biggest wins of his career.

A breakout performance from Ziggler that should have resulted in a sustained main event push, the unforgettable debut of Sting, and a match-long storyline that carried huge stakes helped make this one of the best in event history.

He is almost single-handedly responsible for the 2003 showdown between "Stone Cold" Steve Austin's team and Eric Bischoff's squad for control of Raw.

Michaels led a team of The Dudley Boys, Rob Van Dam and Booker T into action against Randy Orton, Mark Henry, Chris Jericho, Christian and Scott Steiner.

Despite a team of Hall of Famers, Austin's team faced a tremendous deficit midway through the match as The Heartbreak Kid was left to combat Christian, Jericho and Orton on his own.

Bloodied and battered, Michaels showed tremendous heart as he picked off Captain Charisma with Sweet Chin Music and sent Y2J packing by countering his Walls of Jericho into a rollup.

Michaels had the fans invested in his performance, thanks to his body language and selling. They believed in his plight, wanted to see him overcome one last Superstar, preserve Austin's role as Raw general manager and end Bischoff's oppressive rule.

Unfortunately for them, Batista interfered, put an end to Michaels' furious comeback, and ensured the heels would emerge victorious.

One of the great, probably underrated performances of Michaels' entire in-ring comeback, it was proof of the power of a believable underdog babyface in relation to the crowd's willingness to completely invest themselves and become engrossed in the story unfolding before them.

The Invasion storyline ended not with a bang, but a whimper at the 2001 Survivor Series, at least creatively, as eight of the 10 warring competitors in the night's main event were WWE Superstars and only two were WCW or ECW wrestlers acquired at the demise of those two companies.

Still, it was arguably the most star-studded matchup in Survivor Series history. The Rock, Chris Jericho, Kane, Undertaker and Big Show represented the home team against the invading faction, which featured "Stone Cold" Steve Austin, Kurt Angle, Rob Van Dam, Booker T and Shane McMahon.

Much of the build was centered around two stories: could Rock and Jericho coexist long enough to lead WWE to victory, and who was the mole Vince McMahon supposedly had within the Alliance locker room?

The first was answered with a resounding "no," as Jericho, freshly eliminated by Austin, dropped his rival with a Breakdown and left him to battle Austin in a reprisal of their rivalry.

The second came in the closing moments of the match as Angle blasted Austin with the WWE Championship to set up a come-from-behind win for The Rock and WWE.

A great match with heavy storyline involvement throughout, this was a fitting conclusion to the hugely botched Invasion storyline and set up the crowning of an Undisputed WWE Champion at Vengeance the following month.

The star power, the stakes, peak Austin and Rock, the last vestiges of the Attitude Era, and a red-hot crowd came together to create an instant classic and the best traditional Survivor Series elimination tag match of its kind.

articles.title: Las cuentas del número 1 femenino de 2026: Gemma Triay y Delfi Brea pueden cerrarlo en Dubai
articles.standfirst: La pelea por el trono del pádel femenino está que arde
articles.summary: La pelea por el trono del pádel femenino está que arde
articles.body: La lucha por terminar la temporada 2026 en lo más alto del pádel femenino entra en su fase decisiva. Gemma Triay y Delfi Brea llegan al Dubai P1 como líderes de la Race de Premier Padel y con una oportunidad de oro para dejar prácticamente sentenciado el número uno mundial. Sin embargo, el crecimiento de Ari Sánchez y Andrea Ustero durante las últimas semanas ha cambiado el escenario y obliga a las actuales dominadoras a no perder de vista a sus perseguidoras. La pareja hispano-argentina encabeza la clasificación con 14.020 puntos, una renta importante respecto a sus principales rivales. Ari Sánchez y Andrea Ustero ocupan la segunda posición con 11.240 puntos, mientras que Paula Josemaría y Bea González cierran el grupo de las principales aspirantes con 10.340. De esta manera, la diferencia entre las líderes y sus perseguidoras es de 2.780 y 3.680 puntos, respectivamente. El gran momento de Ari y Andrea ha sido uno de los factores que ha devuelto la emoción a la pelea. Sus victorias en París, Róterdam y Milán, junto con los resultados obtenidos frente a Triay y Brea en sus enfrentamientos directos, han permitido reducir una distancia que parecía mucho más difícil de recortar. Ahora, el Dubai P1 se presenta como una prueba fundamental para comprobar si esa remontada puede tener continuidad. El torneo reparte 1.000 puntos a la pareja campeona, una cantidad que puede resultar decisiva teniendo en cuenta que, después de esta cita, únicamente quedarán el México Major y las Premier Padel Finals de Barcelona, con otros 3.500 puntos en juego entre ambas competiciones. Gemma Triay y Delfi Brea tienen una posibilidad real de asegurar matemáticamente el liderato en Dubái, aunque para conseguirlo necesitan combinar su propio triunfo con un resultado concreto de sus principales rivales. El primer requisito es levantar el título, lo que les permitiría añadir 1.000 puntos a su casillero actual. Así, pasarían de los 14.020 puntos que tienen actualmente a un total de 15.020. Pero no sería suficiente con ganar. También necesitarían que Ari Sánchez y Andrea Ustero no consiguieran superar los cuartos de final. En ese supuesto, las segundas clasificadas sumarían 180 puntos, alcanzando los 11.420. La diferencia entre ambas parejas quedaría entonces en 3.600 puntos, una ventaja que superaría los 3.500 puntos que todavía estarían disponibles en las dos últimas citas del calendario. De cumplirse este escenario, Triay y Brea se proclamarían matemáticamente números uno de 2026, ya que sus perseguidoras no tendrían margen para alcanzarles en las competiciones restantes. La situación cambiaría si Ari Sánchez y Andrea Ustero consiguieran alcanzar las semifinales del Dubai P1. En ese caso, sumarían 360 puntos y elevarían su puntuación hasta los 11.600. Aunque Gemma y Delfi consiguieran igualmente el título y alcanzasen los 15.020 puntos, la diferencia entre ambas parejas sería de 3.420 puntos. Una distancia que todavía permitiría a las perseguidoras soñar con el liderato, puesto que quedarían 3.500 puntos por repartir. Por tanto, las actuales líderes no podrían cerrar matemáticamente la clasificación en Dubái y tendrían que esperar al desenlace de los últimos torneos del año. Para Ari y Andrea, alcanzar las semifinales supondría mantener viva la pelea y trasladar toda la presión a las siguientes semanas. Un escalón por detrás aparecen Paula Josemaría y Bea González. La pareja suma 10.340 puntos y se encuentra a 3.680 de la primera posición. Sus opciones son más complicadas, aunque todavía pueden aspirar a mejorar su situación en la clasificación. Incluso en el mejor escenario posible para ellas en Dubái, conquistando el título y sumando los 1.000 puntos disponibles, alcanzarían los 11.340 puntos. Si Triay y Brea también ganasen el torneo, la diferencia entre ambas duplas sería de 3.680 puntos. Una distancia superior a los 3.500 puntos que quedarían por disputarse, por lo que Paula y Bea no podrían alcanzar a las líderes si se produjera ese escenario. La Race femenina todavía tiene tres grandes pruebas por delante, con una importante cantidad de puntos en juego: - Dubai P1: 1.000 puntos para las campeonas. - México Major: 2.000 puntos para las campeonas. - Premier Padel Finals de Barcelona: 1.500 puntos para las campeonas. Gemma Triay y Delfi Brea parten con ventaja y dependen de sus propios resultados para alcanzar el objetivo. Sin embargo, el rendimiento reciente de Ari Sánchez y Andrea Ustero ha añadido emoción a una pelea que parecía más encaminada meses atrás.
